> Direct bleeding anyone at any time is the great equalizer. If you don't
> like what someone's doing (eg RtoI), then go and kill him. I can no
> longer do this with 7/7 RTR. Nuf said.

"Bleed anyone" is not supported by the rulebook (the Jyhad, the
corrected Jyhad, and the VTES rulebooks do not allow for cross-
table bleed).

The errata that gave the (D) symbol the power to freely direct a
bleed at any player has been removed.

But, of course, you can still bleed anyone (except yourself) if card
text allows it (superior Cat Burglary, Kindred Spirits).

Messages.Author: cbo...@apdi.net
Messages.Body:
I don't even know why I'm bothering to post. It seems like any message
that is anti-(6/23 & 7/7)-rulings is just brushed off.

> > Direct bleeding anyone at any time is the great equalizer. If you don't
> > like what someone's doing (eg RtoI), then go and kill him. I can no
> > longer do this with 7/7 RTR. Nuf said.

No, sorry. It's _not_ "Nuf said".

> You can "directly" vote him to death (especially when others think the
>same way you do).
> Vote & Rush & Combat decks become more IMPORTANT with 7/7 rulings.

Ok. And this is good how? I thought that one of biggest assets this game had
was "balance". How is it balanced that any archetype is "more important"
than another? _Why_ should any deck archetype be any more important than
another? It shouldn't, but with the new rulings, they clearly are. Both
Political and Bleed decks are now significantly weaker. However, I'm only
going to discuss the Bleed deck here.

Situation:
You are playing a Bleed deck. Your predator is playing a Political deck and
your prey is playing a Combat deck. A few turns into the game, your pred
starts turning up the heat and calls KRC after KRC after KRC.

Situation: Same as above, except that your predator is now a Combat deck and
your prey is a Political deck. A few turns into the game, your pred starts
attacking and torporizing your vamps.

Pre 7/7 -
To defend yourself, you could back bleed your predator to either inspire
them to turn down the heat or oust them outright, thus giving yourself a
little bit of breathing room.

Post 7/7 -
To defend yourself, you have to start including cards that are anti-vote
and anti-combat. Not in and of itself a bad thing. Most Bleed decks
already include cards like Obedience, Majesty and Delaying Tactics.
However, before, the number of slots those took up in an average bleed
deck was kinda low because they could also be coupled with the back
bleeding strategy. Since the number was low, it didn't interfere much
with the consistancy of the deck. Now, though, in order to mount any
kind of defense against a Combat or Political deck, the number of
those cards in your deck must increase significantly and as such,
significantly water down the deck. When you also include defenses
for bleed decks, such as Deflection, etc., the deck become almost
unworkable.
Basically, it comes down to either: Have a consistant deck, sacrificing
any measurable defense against all 3 archetypes OR Have a measurable
defense, sacrificing consistancy.

A Combat deck can affect any methuselah at the table. If it's predator
is breathing down their neck too hard, it can torpor one or more of the
predator's vampires thus slowing the predator down. A Political deck
can affect any methuselah at the table. It can vote to oust it's predator
if it's predator is becoming too great a threat. Why is it that a Bleed
deck should have the major disadvantage of never being able to directly
affect a threatening predator?
Well, I guess I shouldn't say "Never". There are those cards: 'Night
Moves', 'Cat Burglary' and 'Kindred Spirits'. I almost forgot about those.
Why? Because they are forgettable. Both 'Night Moves' and 'Cat
Burglary' limit the bleed to 1 maximum, period, ever. A 1 bleed is going
to affect your predator very little if at all. In the case of 'Kindred
Spirits',why should I be limited to 1 clan if I want the ability to defend
against a powerful predator. That seems rather limiting to me and I thought
that another thing that people liked about the game was that it had near
*unlimited* possibilities.

Now, I can already hear the responses to this post:
"LSJ is god and LSJ knows all and what LSJ says is law"

or

"Well, that's what it says in the rulebook and the rulebook is right".

I've nothing to say to the former since sticking your fingers in your
ears and going "lalalalalalalalalalalalala" serves no purpose or good.
However, to the latter, I have this to say:
If the designers of the game were infallable with all the aspects of the
game, from the rulebook to the cards, then why errata any of the cards?
Why change any of the rules? Since many of the cards/rules have been
errata'd/changed (going so far as to outright change the card text), it
is obvious that you don't think the desingers were infallable. Since the
designers were apparently wrong about many of the cards/rules,
couldn't they have been wrong about the (D) bleed issue as well? Or
even the 1 PA/action?
While I deplore many of the recent card changes, if both of these rulings
were to be reversed, I'd be happy. But then, it's not like anything I say
matters...

Sorrow

anymore |--------------------------------

anymore | you never seen anyone try to
I don't need a reason to kill myself | commit suicide before?" - Anon

Well, bleed decks are inherently a stronger archetype. If a bleed deck
succeeds in an action, its prey is closer to be ousted. In general, no one
on the table other than its prey can interfere with that action.
Contrast that with a vote deck. If a vote deck succeeds in an action,
its prey might be closer to being ousted. Other people on the table can
interfere with that action pretty trivially.
Contrast that with a combat deck. If a combat deck succeeds in an
action, its prey might be out a vampire. She still has as much pool as she
did previously. Even if a combat deck torporizes all its prey's vampires,
it still has to bleed out the pool without being bled out itself.
And I thought you said that the Immortal Grapple rulings made combat
decks weaker, too? If everyone got weakened, what's the problem?

>Pre 7/7 -
>To defend yourself, you could back bleed your predator to either inspire
>them to turn down the heat or oust them outright, thus giving yourself a
>little bit of breathing room.

Yeah, that's always a thrill for a combat deck. You've walloped on
your predator enough that you can take his maximum bleed for next
turn. You've put enough of your prey's vampires in torpor that he
won't block or deflect you any more and he's letting you bleed him.
Sure, you're tapped out, but its not like you're gonna get bled out anyway.
Oh, whoops, your prey gets to use his Govern the Unaligned not just
to oust his prey, but anyone else on the table he doesn't like. Too
bad for you.
I've never seen anyone "back off" after their prey went upstream,
except in the sense of "goes terminally defensive for the turn it takes
the predator to kill them."

>Post 7/7 -
>To defend yourself, you have to start including cards that are anti-vote
>and anti-combat. Not in and of itself a bad thing. Most Bleed decks

Man, it must be horrible to be building a bleed deck and have to
include defenses. How do you cope?
Everyone has these problems. Balancing offense and defense is
what makes Jyhad deck building interesting.

>A Combat deck can affect any methuselah at the table. If it's predator
>is breathing down their neck too hard, it can torpor one or more of the
>predator's vampires thus slowing the predator down. A Political deck
>can affect any methuselah at the table. It can vote to oust it's predator
>if it's predator is becoming too great a threat. Why is it that a Bleed
>deck should have the major disadvantage of never being able to directly
>affect a threatening predator?

Why should the bleed deck get to eliminate its prey's pool directly
without interference from the table?

[Snip a bunch of straw men]

>While I deplore many of the recent card changes, if both of these rulings
>were to be reversed, I'd be happy. But then, it's not like anything I say
>matters...

Well, since you said you were out of here a couple of weeks ago,
I suppose what you say doesn't even matter to yourself.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
cbo...@apdi.net wrote:
>
> I don't even know why I'm bothering to post. It seems like any message
> that is anti-(6/23 & 7/7)-rulings is just brushed off.

Posts without coherent points are brushed off. It just seems that
lately many of the anti-new-rulings posts have been not-so-coherent.

> Situation:
> You are playing a Bleed deck. Your predator is playing a Political deck and
> your prey is playing a Combat deck. A few turns into the game, your pred
> starts turning up the heat and calls KRC after KRC after KRC.
>
> Situation: Same as above, except that your predator is now a Combat deck and
> your prey is a Political deck. A few turns into the game, your pred starts
> attacking and torporizing your vamps.
>
> Pre 7/7 -
> To defend yourself, you could back bleed your predator to either inspire
> them to turn down the heat or oust them outright, thus giving yourself a
> little bit of breathing room.

This isn't really defending yourself. It's just plain unproductive.
It's your predator's job to kill you. If you start bleeding her, it
will be her job to kill you _faster_ to stay alive. If you oust your
predator, you get no victory point, and you get a brand new predator,
with 6 more pool, who will _also_ want to kill you. I have never seen
random cross-table bleedings help anyone win a game.

> Post 7/7 -
> To defend yourself, you have to start including cards that are anti-vote
> and anti-combat.

Gasp! God forbid that you put defenses in your deck like everyone
else! A deck without combat defense will die against a combat deck. A
deck without vote defense will die against a vote deck.

In a Rush deck, the bleed defense is "kill the bleeders". This works
only in a very broad sense. You want to weaken your predator enough so
that they don't kill you very fast, and you don't want to weaken them so
much that they're ousted by _their_ predator.

> Basically, it comes down to either: Have a consistant deck, sacrificing
> any measurable defense against all 3 archetypes OR Have a measurable
> defense, sacrificing consistancy.

You're saying you want all of your decks to be One-Trick Ponies. You
don't want to have to put in defenses because they make your deck less
effective. But without _any_ defenses, your deck is _much_ less
effective, since it can be easily thwarted.

> A Combat deck can affect any methuselah at the table. If it's predator
> is breathing down their neck too hard, it can torpor one or more of the
> predator's vampires thus slowing the predator down.

This is because that's what a combat deck does. It really doesn't work
as effectively as you seem to think. It takes a great deal of finesse.
You're talking about using a sledgehammer (big cross-table bleeds) to
take care of your deck's inherent weaknesses.

> A Political deck
> can affect any methuselah at the table. It can vote to oust it's predator
> if it's predator is becoming too great a threat. Why is it that a Bleed
> deck should have the major disadvantage of never being able to directly
> affect a threatening predator?

A deck should never oust its predator. A deck which consistently has to
bleed its predator to defend itself is flawed.

> Now, I can already hear the responses to this post:
> "LSJ is god and LSJ knows all and what LSJ says is law"
>
> or
>
> "Well, that's what it says in the rulebook and the rulebook is right".

Or, my response: cross-table bleeding was never that effective anyway,
and only served to perpetuate the "gang up on the guy who's winning"
mentality which is indicative of many multiplayer games, but not this
one.

James
--

ham...@math.wisc.edu

Messages.Author: Ethan Burrow
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:

> This isn't really defending yourself. It's just plain unproductive.
> It's your predator's job to kill you. If you start bleeding her, it
> will be her job to kill you _faster_ to stay alive. If you oust your
> predator, you get no victory point, and you get a brand new predator,
> with 6 more pool, who will _also_ want to kill you. I have never seen
> random cross-table bleedings help anyone win a game.

Random Cross bleeding doesn't, but well timed bleeds on a real threat do. Let me
give you an example :

I have an Assamite/Toreador Bruise Bleed deck that works quite nicely. It doesn't
have strong intercept or much vote defense, but I was able to use my Social
charms/Legal Manipulations to help take out a predator I couldn't handle with the
cards in my hand. The next predator usually could be blocked and/or dealt with so
I refocused on my prey.

With the new rulings I will likely have to add Surprise Influence and a little
rush to my deck, which in the long run will dilute my deck strategy....but
necessary to become competitive with the new 7/7 rulings.

I'm not necessarily whining about not having direct bleeds, but I'd rather have it
back than dilute my deck. I have bled my predator out several times and in all
cases; I continued to play to gain a victory point instead of dying at the hands
of the previous predator.

--
Ethan Burrow
Prince of Austin

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 7 Aug 1998, Ethan Burrow wrote:

> I have an Assamite/Toreador Bruise Bleed deck that works quite nicely.
> It doesn't have strong intercept or much vote defense, but I was able to
> use my Social charms/Legal Manipulations to help take out a predator I
> couldn't handle with the cards in my hand. The next predator usually
> could be blocked and/or dealt with so I refocused on my prey.

Let's see. You are saying that your deck design has difficulty dealing
with a single determined predator, and you would prefer not to have to do
that. I would say it is a good thing for you that your own prey is not a
determined back-bleeder, because then your deck would have to deal with
*two* predators, when you cannot even handle one.

> With the new rulings I will likely have to add Surprise Influence and a
> little rush to my deck, which in the long run will dilute my deck
> strategy....but necessary to become competitive with the new 7/7
> rulings.

It will also give your predator a snowball's chance in hell to win the
game. That's fair, I think. It will also give your Assamite/Toreador B&B
deck a chance to win should you end up behind a bleed deck rather than in
front of one.

> I'm not necessarily whining about not having direct bleeds, but I'd
> rather have it back than dilute my deck. I have bled my predator out
> several times and in all cases;

In all cases? This sounds like too much of a good think for you and too
much of a bad thing for him. His only crime was that he is a better
player than your grand-predator. Had he been a bad player, you would have
left him alone, but he still would have lost.

It was the same with my own back-bleeding dramatic upheaval deck. Whether
the strategy worked or not, my predator was *always* ousted first. His
fate was sealed the moment seating was picked. Do you think that's right?

> I continued to play to gain a victory
> point instead of dying at the hands of the previous predator.

That's nice. But it's an awful good thing for you that the guy you
eventually ousted did not start back-bleeding you to prevent this from
happening. From what you have told me, it sounds as though your deck has
no means of dealing with such a strategy. You have trouble dealing with
ONE predator, much less two.

But I don't think *anyone* can deal with two determined bleeders, and I
don't think they should have to.

If I may intercede here, I think that there is a little miscommunication:
Crosstable bleed _is_ a defence of /sorts/. Not in the traditional sense,
that by defence means improving your own ability to repel an attack, but by
reducing your opponents ability to attack.

Clarification: by bleeding another player other than your prey, you reduce
their primary resource (pool) and they have (should) devote more of their
secondary resources (vampires) to defend their primary resource (pool).
Therefore a crosstable bleed is, after a fashion, a defensive action as it
depletes the targetted methuselah's offensive resources because they need a
higher proportion of defensive resources.

Naturally, this statement falls apart when you have a player who has a purely
offensive deck - or a player who considers that the _only_ defense is a good
offense.

> > That's why you don't Cross-Table bleed randomly.
>

> I use the word "random" in a very broad sense. To me, any ct-bleed is
> "random".

Then you are misusing the word. Random does mean "without cause or reason" as
in a "random victim". Perhaps you mean something else. ("extraneous"? as in
bleeds extraneous to the primary purpose?)

At this point, I should probably note that I am actually _not_ in favour of
ct-bleeds, but I do understand the argument. I'll get to my reasons for not
supporting ct-bleeding presently.

>
> > Most stealth/
> > bleed decks will not include much voting power. With the threat
> > of (D) bleeds you can Politic a Political deck into reducing the
> > level of agression.
>

> No, you can't. If you start bleeding me from across the table, I will
> have no choice but to attack you harder just to stay alive. Even if you
> are across the table, it's better to give your predator a victory point
> than allow you to oust me.

This is not necessarily true - it is a rare event to see a jyhad game
degenerate into a ct melee (unless there are out of game reasons)(at least
locally). The usual result of an exchange like this is that the opponents
come to some sort of understanding - at least temporarily, while they build
up for the next attack.. Given a playgroup (or even a reasonably
communicative tournament), armstice can be reached.

Reagardless of this, a true ct bleed (ie, not your predator) will result in
retaliation of some description, and usually will not serve the acting
methuselah well - unless it was a decisive blow (ie near oust or oust), in
which case it does not serve the purpose of a warning, and only results in
the strengthening of another methuselah (most likely prey).

>
> > >Gasp! God forbid that you put defenses in your deck like everyone
> > >else! A deck without combat defense will die against a combat deck. A
> > >deck without vote defense will die against a vote deck.

This is true... to a degree. A deck with a sufficiently strong offense can
make it a defense of sorts - through intimidation or other means.

> > ie.. If you don't target me with that vote, I won't bleed you for a lot..
>

> OK, if you're not my prey, why would I be targetting you with a lot of
> damage from that vote anyway?

Because you might be my grand prey, and I'm about to dispose of my current
prey. Example: one of the standard KRC distributions : 3 to prey, 1 to grand
prey.

> > Granted, it's harder for the combat deck to typically pull this off. But a
> > S&B deck that's focusing on someone else besides their prey won't gain any
> > victory points. Last I looked, that's how you determine who's ahead in the
> > game.
>

> Well, I have been told repeatedly that the person who is ahead is the
> one with lots of pool and/or minions, and that person must be ganged up
> on and stopped at all costs.

Are you supporting this position or not? It seems to be a strange one...

My take on the whole issue:
There are three basic types of strategy (I'm not going to go into hybrids or
implementation): Bleed, Combat and Vote. These strategies pursue the primary
goal (removal of primary resource (pool)) through different means. Bleed
directly targets the primary resource, as _can_ vote. The difference between
these two strategies is the ability of other decks to interfere (other vote
decks can directly interfere with voting, as compared to (D) bleed, which only
the target (prey) may prevent). Combat is alone in its ability to _directly_
target secondary resources (vampires + minions).

So while combat can target _only_ secondary resources, it has the trade off
of being able to target _any_ methuselahs secondary resources. Bleed (and
vote) which can directly target primary resources (pool) can only affect it's
prey. To me, this is the balance - versatility versus power. Paradoxically,
this means that combat decks may be the strongest defensively :)

Let me clarify; there's a difference between "offense as defense" and a
"proactive defense". A proactive defense seeks to kill/incapacitate
those minions that might act against you before they can do so. This
type of defense is used primarily by combat decks since they (a) have to
devote so much deck space to combat cards and (b) usually don't have the
right disciplines to have the more standard reactive defenses (bounce,
reduction). So in a rush deck, you are good at one and only one thing:
beating people up. While in theory this is a sufficient tactic to defend
against bleed and vote, in practice this is really hard to pull off.

> Because you might be my grand prey, and I'm about to dispose of my current

One is not a lot of damage.

> > one with lots of pool and/or minions, and that person must be ganged up
> > on and stopped at all costs.
>
> Are you supporting this position or not? It seems to be a strange one...

trying to win don't go jumping all over one deck on the table. Very
often there is collusion between a deck's predator and prey, but beyond
that, an "entire table gang-up" is rare and almost always irrational.

I had been told a couple of months ago that in one person's group when
an Ivory Bow came into play the entire table went into a mad frenzy to
destroy it. I just don't understand that kind of paranoia.

C.B. was not fixed in the reprinting (at least, not without further
errata). As printed (under the pre-7/7 concept of "what makes a directed
action directed?"), inferior C.B. is an undirected action (see: no (D)
symbol, which used to be required for a card-bases action to be
directed).

> It seems to me that changing the nature of (D) will simply create more
> confusion/chaos in an already complex play environ.

So that the rules as they have always been printed will apply?
Hardly confusing.

with slow build-up decks. But why sit around building up when you can
be killing your prey?

I think aggressive play evolves when everyone decides that they're
trying to win. Spending lots of time "consolidating resources" doesn't
make you win unless everyone's doing that. I think aggressiveness
versus nonaggressiveness has more to do with attitude and nothing to do
with gun decks.

Slow build-up decks die because they spend lots of time sitting around
putting equipment on their minions and hunting and so on. Adrian
Sullivan's GenCon deck is possibly an exception, but he has lots of
cards in his deck designed to make people ignore him and beat each other
up while he takes time to set up.

I would caution against using the term ethic as ethics imply that there is a
right and wrong (or at least more right and more wrong). A better term would
be game style.

> In a group where all the players are trying to win, why would they not
> play aggressively? It seems that here is our dilemma; you seem to play
> with slow build-up decks. But why sit around building up when you can
> be killing your prey?

Weenie decks are easier to be at least semi-effective because of their
quickness. A deck that uses larger vampires is harder to construct because
you have a lot more to worry about (vampire fragility, number of actions
you'll be able to take, having enough vampires to block and to act, etc.)
If your slow build up decks are _always_ losing to aggressive weenie speed
decks, then you need to reword your deck. And even when you do, it is very
difficult to get more wins against a speed deck.

easy to steal, destroy, or take by diablerie.

> Slow build-up decks die because they spend lots of time sitting around
> putting equipment on their minions and hunting and so on. Adrian
> Sullivan's GenCon deck is possibly an exception, but he has lots of
> cards in his deck designed to make people ignore him and beat each other

I recently put together the ol' Alexandra and Toreador Grand Ball deck
for use in my playgroup. The first game, I never drew a TGB, and got
wiped out by combat (had rushed to make the deck and left out combat defense).
In the second try, I got a TGB out quickly, and there was no intercept on
the table.

One of the best cards to help out a slow deck is Millicent Smith. She's a
great deterrent. If you're having trouble against speed decks, put in a
couple (and a couple intercept permanents if you don't have them), and you'll
increase the survival rate of your slow decks.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
"davey! hathorn" <dhat...@midway.uchicago.edu> wrote:

> LSJ wrote:
> > Section 15, Contested Cards
> > Third paragraph should say "You can't bring out more than one of the
> > same unique card into your active region without contesting them."
>
> In the event that someone actually wanted to do this, how much blood
> would they spend? What if I am self-contesting Lupo, and my preditor
> brings out a Lupo of his own? Who pays how much? Lastly, after I let
> go of one of my Lupo-copies, my prey brings one out as well. Now how
> much do we pay?

The cost to contest any card is one pool. During your you either pay this
cost or yield the card. The decision to pay the cost or yield is made
individually for each card you are contesting.

If you have two cards which you are contesting (two of the same - Lupo,
for example - or two different), then you can either pay two pool to
continue contesting both of them, pay one to contest one and yield the
other, or pay nothing and yield both.

Same for your prey - she pays one pool for each card she is contesting,
regardless of how many other copies of that card other Methuselahs have
(also contested).

If you are self-contesting (two copies of) Lupo and your predator is
contesting (one copy of) Lupo as well, the you would have to burn two
pool during your untap to keep contesting both copies, or pay one pool
and yield one copy, or pay nothing and yield both copies. Your predator
(if Lupo is still being contested) would have to burn one pool during
her untap to continue contesting or pay nothing and yield.

--

Au contraire, mein freund. The game of Jyhad or V:tES does specify a
particular target for each methuselah. Even in the RPG, (take CbN as an
example) most methuselahs have one particular enemy. In the CCG, this is
altered slightly to allow for multiplayer games by having a prey and a
predator - one person you are supposed to attack, and one you are supposed to
defend from. If you do not accept this premise, we are not playing the same
game, and can't discuss the relative merits of rules, and I'll stop badgering
you :)

If you do accept the notion of prey and predator, then ct-bleeding cannot be
a part of the game because of a number of reasons, pre-eminent among are the
following: * ct-bleeds do _not_ aid the acting methuselah. This is an
established fact. At best they create a situation where you weaken another
methuselah who is anot your prey (and who has little to no chance of
defending), which will result in retaliation of some form or another. At
worst you will oust another methuselah, granting pool and VPs to another
methuselah who will soon be your prey or predator * ct-bleeds disrupt the
game dynamic. The predator-prey relationship creates a unique game unlike
other CCGs. ct-bleeds disrupt the cycle, to no discernable advantage. In
fact, it usually creates a disadvantage to one or more methuselahs.
*ct-bleeds directly target the pool of another methuselah. This should not be
allowed because bleeds are the most powerful (direct) means of winning the
game, and should not have the versatility of other strategies that have less
direct ousting power *and finally, ct-bleeds are _not_ part of the original
or revised game.

> a concern than winning the game. "Gee, I'd better not worry about my
> predator and that other guy across from me. I just wanna get my victory

No, you do worry about your predator. But ct-bleeds against your predator do
_not_ assist your defence - if anything they weaken your position, because
your predator must cease defending and go all out on attack, because he/she
cannot hope to defend against two opponents.

And if anything, I doubt this is "boring". It is a tense, stress filled
situation where you are racing to oust your prey before your predator can
target oust you.

> I'd rather win the whole game, than ousting my prey. Afterall,

You can only win the game _by_ ousting your prey.

> tournaments are where the game is played for the most part.

I doubt it. I'd think it highly likely that far more game are played in
playgroups than official tournaments. And furthermore, I'm not quite sure what
this statement has to do with your argument...

> to bleed anyone you want as they are contesting with you for dominance
> of the game.

Richard Garfield intended Jyhad to not have too much interaction
(because those kinds of game pretty much suck!) and decided to only
allows bleeds of your prey. His WoD tidbit was that while all the
Methuselahs were at war with each other each still had a particular
public enemy number one that they focussed on. Since non-directable
bleeds is the original intention of the game, I find arguments in favor
of omni-directable bleeds about as meaningful as a thread about why
having 3 Master Phase Actions per turn would make the game better.

> I think too many of you play tournaments where getting points is more of
> a concern than winning the game. "Gee, I'd better not worry about my
> predator and that other guy across from me. I just wanna get my victory
> point for ousting my prey and stay in as long as I can so I can get some
> more points." Boring.

What are you talking about? The "points" you mention are Victory
Points! You get victory points by taking out prey. You get to the
finals by getting lots of VPs and not by trying to make it to the
time-limit just so you can gain a half-VP.

> I'd rather win the whole game, than ousting my prey. Afterall,
> tournaments are where the game is played for the most part.

Right. Win the whole game by ousting the most prey.

>I agree whole heartedly with Badger!!! It's crazy to get rid of this wonderful
>action. How nice it is to get back at someone fora wrong doing. Or use it
>just to start some FUN with someone.
>

*sigh*

How likely is it that someone will hit you cross-table with a rush? A
rush deck has enough problems of its own to hit someone cross-table
without provocation.

How likely is it that someone will hit you cross-table with a vote?
Well, vote decks have their own problems with No Vote Pushing (which I
whole-heartedly support) meaning that if they *can* get a vote passed,
they'll be much better off using it on prey, predator and, possibly,
grand-prey. Unless provoked, there is very little reason for cross-
table votes.

How likely is that someone will bleed you cross-table? Well, a bleed
deck is going to be better off ousting your prey with your cards and
getting the blood and the victory points. Unless provoked, there is
very little reason for cross-table bleeds.

Unfortunately, the biggest provocation on the table is *another* cross-
table bleed from a spiteful player, who would rather oust you than their
prey, simple because you're playing well, have a good deck, have a lot
of VPs so far (in a tournament). Like I said, a cross-table rush is
VERY risky any of the time. You can't afford the vamps. A cross-table
vote is now a lot less likely if you can't empty your hand of vote cards
for it. A cross-table bleed is the only action that can be reliably
pulled off.

Cross-table bleeds beget cross-table bleeds.

In article, ve...@nospam.demon.co.uk says...

>How likely is it that someone will hit you cross-table with a rush? A
>rush deck has enough problems of its own to hit someone cross-table
>without provocation.

A cross-table rush can be very handy indeed. Rushing a Methuselah before he
becomes your predator or prey in can be a smart move. Sometimes rushing that
voter before he or she casts another vote that will buttress one's prey or
predator can mean the difference between survival and being ousted.

>How likely is it that someone will hit you cross-table with a vote?
>Well, vote decks have their own problems with No Vote Pushing (which I
>whole-heartedly support) meaning that if they *can* get a vote passed,
>they'll be much better off using it on prey, predator and, possibly,
>grand-prey. Unless provoked, there is very little reason for cross-
>table votes.

How many have been in a game and been vicitimized by voters who see you as a
threat but are not your predator or prey? I saw a shrewd cross-table Banishment
vote turn the tide in a JOL game. Pool gaining votes are common and may assist
your predator or prey. To me, a vote affecting one's grand-prey qualifies as a
"cross-table" vote.

>Cross-table bleeds beget cross-table bleeds.

Poor strategy is not a reason to ban an action; that the game was originally
designed not to have cross-table bleeding is a compelling reason (to me at least).
However, I did like having cross-table bleeding. Using bleeds to slow down your
predator was an infrequent, but effective and valid defensive tactic. In my view,
if one can freely bounce bleeds than one should be able to bleed whomever one
wants. The argument that there is a lack of defense to a cross-table bleed applies
similarly to bounces (but bounces are not so restricted).

passed, they'll be much better off using it on prey, predator and,

vote deck, but if that means that they end up dictating the terms, I

torporised by his prey's copy of Richter), I'll be much better off
attacking those people close to me rather than cross-table, unless,
perhaps in extenuating circumstances, I could possibly get rid of the
other vote deck and oust it. OF course, other people on the table have
votes and might defend it - people colluding with it to use Anathema,
say.

Now, in a roughly equal position, dropping a point or two on a cross-
table Methuselah is possible to try and get the co-operation of the
other vote deck, but the majority still has to go to someone directly
affecting me or the point of my calling the vote is pretty minimal.

Messages.Author: badger
Messages.Body:
Why?

Rush/combat decks can target anyone they want. Political decks can
target anyone they want. To some extent, you can intercept anyone you
want (Eagle Sight, Anneke, etc). Therefore, I should be able to bleed
ANYONE I want to. Why is bleeding being handicapped?

Case in point:
Last night I was playing Jyhad. I had your prototypical stealth/bleed
deck working. My predator had a rush/combat deck. Immediately he set
upon my vamps, working them over. I had no defense against this, EXCEPT
to direct bleed him! So I did. And you know what? He backed off -
giving me valuable time to recoup. (If I could have, I would've bled
him out because I had no fear of his predator even if she gained the six
blood for his ousting because I had plenty of bleed bounce/reduction to
hold her off.) As the game wore on, he became distracted with his
predator and I was finally able to go on the offensive. I eliminated my
prey with bleeds totalling seven. My predator was eliminated with a
bounced RTI (oooohhh!) - not mine - before my next turn.

So his predator was now after me (Toreador Presence bleed deck). As I
said, I could hold her off, but I was low on pool - so not for long as
my deck is primarily offensive and I had just influenced a new vamp.
What to do? My new prey had only three pool left and my Tor predator
2. A fame had been played and that vamp was in torpor. I could
eliminate my prey as I had just enough strength to get through, but in
doing so I would leave myself wide open for elimination by the
Toreadors. Sure I could secure another "victory point", but I like
winning and this was no tournament.

Here's what I did - I bled my prey down to one and with my last
remaining vamp, I (Oh, NO - call the RTR!!) DIRECT bled my predator to 1
also. I ended my turn. My prey was eliminated via the Fame and so was
my predator. I got the point AND I stayed in the game. My new predator
didn't scare me as he had only 1 vamp out and I still had a blocker with
reduction potential.

So you see, direct bleeding kept me in the game early by warning my
rushing predator off and it secured my second place finish in the 8 man
game we were playing.

Without direct bleeding I would've been dead in the first few rounds and
would've sat there for the next 2 hrs while everyone else played. So
don't tell me direct bleeding is a gang-up strategy, or for sore losers,
or has no place in the game.

It is a viable offensive and defensive strategy.

Badger

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <35E0412B...@buffnet.net>, badger <bad...@buffnet.net>
writes

>Why?
>
>Rush/combat decks can target anyone they want. Political decks can
>target anyone they want. To some extent, you can intercept anyone you
>want (Eagle Sight, Anneke, etc). Therefore, I should be able to bleed
>ANYONE I want to. Why is bleeding being handicapped?

Rush/combat incapacitates a minion, not pool.

Political affects pool but EVERYONE can vote.

Intercept is not pro-active. People can get round intercept
(unblockability, actions that don't care if they're blocked - combat
etc.). Intercept can only affect minions, not pool.

Bleed affects pool and only one person can stop it. If it goes cross-
table, still only one person can stop it - and not a person who was
expecting to get hit by you.

*sigh*

Bleed: gets rid of pool (unlike combat)
doesn't interact with whole table (unlike vote)

So: it can only affect your prey.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Badger wrote:
"Very likely, if that person is playing politics and just voted to steal
your location. Very likely if that person is playing politics and calls peace
treaty to burn you weapons. Very likely, if they vote to burn your allies.
Very likely, if that person just mind raped one of your minions. Very likely,
if that person just Malk Dem you. Need I go on?"

Provoking someone across the table is idiocy, tournament or no. Jyhad is a
game where the people next to you are your enemies and the people not next to
you are your (for the time being) friends. For the vast bulk of the time, you
gain nothing at all by acting against the people across the table from you, and
usually weaken your position in the long run, as this sort of activity
invariably strengthens your enemies (the people sitting next to you). Voting
to hurt someone across the table is dumb. Rushing someone across the table is
dumb. Bleeding someone across the table is dumb. It strengthens your enemies,
wastes your actions, and weakens your position. Never a good idea.

I play Rush decks all the time. I almost never Rush across the table, and the
only times I do is out of spite when I am losing anyway and someone across the
table does something dumb and random, like cross table bleed me.

The more possibility there is in the game for random, spiteful actions like
CTBs, the weaker the game is.

"Jyhad isn't just a tournament game where everyone's worried about VPs.
It 90% played in the shops and living rooms where people want to have

fun and win if they can. And if it takes a direct bleed or 10 to

accomplish that, then so be it."

This has nothing to do with whether you are in a tournament or not. A game
succeeds or fails based on how well it is designed. Anything that comprimises
good design weakens the game. I fail to see why people in shops and living
rooms should be required to play a substandard game. If you want to play with
wacky house rules, by all means, go ahead, but the rules as they currently are
lend to a well designed and well balanced play environment, whether in a
tournament or a living room.

> bleeding him a couple times, but if you were playing a combat defense free S+B
> deck, you should have never taken an action again (as every vampire you get is
> immediately destroyed before it takes a single action) after pulling such a
> feat. What am I missing?

What you are missing is that Jyhad is not a 1D game. People don't go
full offense. If his prey were to use every vampire to kill each of his
each turn, he would have had no defense against the Toreador Bleed Deck
- not a smart move. If this is the *normal* mindset of a "self
respecting Rush deck" then that must be why people are always
complaining they don't win much (I do fine with them when I use them by
the way).

Kevin

Messages.Body:

writes

<snip>

Badger, you live in a world where you attack all over the table,
attacking anyone in sight. You gather no allies in your games and
therefore provide no incentive for anyone to help you. If you're not
playing in a tournament, the reputation you keep as a player is of great
importance. You seem to think that hitting anyone, anywhere on the
table, at any time is a GREAT MOVE!!!

Your arguments are based round "It's fun" and other puerile statements.
If you are quite incapable of seeing that combat decks have enough
problems of their own before they START attacking across a table (as
opposed to retaliate against it), that a vote deck now has a great deal
of trouble securing the votes it needs so is unlikely to START a cross-
table frenzy and that other deck types are generally unstable and
insecure in that, though quite possibly powerful, they often are quite
precariously balanced in what they do and that they have enough problems
of their own without having to start going across table for no reason,
then we are not playing the same game.

A bleed deck has NO problems bleeding cross-table. Bleeding cross-table
is no different to bleeding your prey, from its point of view. It can
still stealth it as much as it likes, increase the bleed as much as it
likes and so forth. A vote deck incurs the wrath of the other votes on
the table, and a vote deck has many fewer votes now. A combat deck
loses the action it should have been taking against its predator to stop
them bleeding/voting against it. A bleed deck loses very little since
it can already do large bleeds against its prey with one action, so
losing an action doesn't matter so much. Bleeding cross-table can often
be a "good" way to cycle cards when they're filling your hand, and the
rules are quite obviously set up to make unnecessary cycling difficult
to do.

>LET Cross Table Bleeds BE!!!
>

*sigh*

Please provide solid arguments of your own. Not just "It's fun" and "We
have to allow them". Give us proper, solid information which shows that
they are not unbalancing, were what the Game Designers intended, do not
allow King-Making in any way and do not disrupt the Predator-Prey
dynamic.

I tell you what, I will give a couple of examples as to why you may want to
perform ct actions (please feel free to add to this list since I do not have
time to type all day).

1. You wish to remove a player that has half of the political muscle when
you have the other half
2. You wish to bring out a vampire without contesting (another player
already has him out)
3. As above but with locations, allies, or any contestable card
4. A person threatens to be your predator soon and you can tell that you
will have a very diffucult time defending vs them

current prey will die) blood, blood, blood

power
10. etc, etc, etc ......

Don't you get it ........ there is no limit to the reasoning for performing ct
actions, it specifically depends upon the game you are playing at the time.
This game is so much more than predator prey interaction, it is specifically
the capability to affect anyone at the table (within certain strictures) that
allow this game to have the depth that so many other CCGs lack. Those across
the table from oneself can either be nominal allies or enemies, in direct
cooperation to aid each other (for a short period) or be totally oblivious to
one another.

The magic mentality of I'm going to max/mini my deck to the point of total
predictablity, narrow focus and short game play with my competitor having no
chance of survival is absolutely moronic. Alright 1 round Jyhad kills yea how
great. Develop a theme yes, build in a "degree" of predictability and play the
game (don't buy as many rare cards as you can just to assure a quick win). Try
bulding combat decks without IG or bums rush. Try building a prescence deck
without majesty. Christ people develop some originality. (Note: If this last
statement applies to you you know who you are, if not my apologies for stating
the obvious).

-Chris

BTW who really cares about VPs, the man still seated at the table with his
toys still alive wins the day.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Kevin Kelly wrote:
"Never is an awful strong word. I agree that it is *usually* not a good idea
take cross-table actions. This statement alone makes me wonder why people are
so adament about eliminating them. By eliminating something which you have
said never helps (I disagree with never) you also stop me from including
something that I think *may* help."

The reason CTBs have been eliminated is because they were not in the original
rules. The concept of omnidirectable (D) bleeds were an abhorrent mistake by
the old rules team, and were not based on the original rules of the game.
Jyhad was designed in such a way that barring a card speciffically saying so
(like Cat Burgalry or Night Moves), you could only bleed your prey, (D) action
or no. The RT decision that changed this was completely erroneous and not
based on any worthwhile decision. It was an error.

That being said, whether or not CTBs are useful are not at issue. My point in
the previous post was that in most cases, acting against someone across the
table is a bad idea. I understand that occasionally a strike across the table
is helpful, if not vital, to winning a particular game. I lost a tournament
final because I was Rushed from across the table at a very inopportune time,
which was inconvinient, but as the situation was, certainly not a random act on
the part of the guy across the table. Yes, occasionally acting across the
table is useful, but more often than not, acting across the table is incredibly
random and is done for not strategically viable reason.

"I you don't think it helps me, WHY DO YOU CARE."

I don't care whether or not it helps you, but in situations where people CTB
for no good reason, it _completely_ screws the guy being assaulted, to the
point where it damages the game for everyone involved. If you CTB me for
spite's sake, you will lose and I will lose. The difference is that you make
the decision to lose the game for yourself, but I do not have the option to
decide not to lose the game.

"I'm saying that sometimes it does help and I may just want to prepare
appropriately for that situation. It is up to the skill of a player to
determine when it is good (seldom) and when
it is detrimental."

Yes, occasionally acting across the table will help you. More often than not,
however, acting across the table is done out of randomocity, spite, or just
plain idiocy. This ruins the game for everyone, not just the two people
involved.

"Don't tell me I can't do it just because *you* don't think it can help me.
(This goes for all forms of cross table actions not just bleeds - I have used
them all at one time or another at a definate help to me)."

I'm not telling you that you can't act across the table. I am telling you that
more often than not it is not a good idea, and anything that reduces the
chances of this occurring improve the game. The reason you can't Bleed across
the table is because it is against the rules.

"While we're at it, lets get ride of
the Chain Saw and the Oxford location from DS"

We did get rid of Chain Saw.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Kevin Kelly wrote:
"What you are missing is that Jyhad is not a 1D game. People don't go full
offense. If his prey were to use every vampire to kill each of his each turn,
he would have had no defense against the Toreador Bleed Deck- not a smart
move."

Any worthwhile Rush deck that is faced with a defenseless S+B deck (such as a
generic Malk deck) will have all the time in the world to kill the Malk
softies, and still have the ability to defend against its Toreador Predator. A
reliable and fast Rush deck should torporize/burn a Malkavian on every action
it takes. Given a well designed Rush deck, a Malkavian prey will never manage
to take an action from turn one, unless the Rush deck lets them. If I have 3
or 4 smallish vampires, I can easily survive by attacking my predator or prey
equally. If my prey decides to back bleed me, I will let my predator alone for
a turn, and destroy every vampire my prey has in his active reigon. It
probably won't hurt me much.

"If this is the *normal* mindset of a "self respecting Rush deck" then that
must be why people are always complaining they don't win much (I do fine with
them when I use them by
the way). "

The normal mindset of a Rush deck is to destroy what threatens you. If your
predator is dangerous, you whack him first. If not, you demolish your prey.
If your prey gets uppity and back bleeds you, you punish him severely for it.
If your Rush deck does not have this ability, then you are playing an
ineffective Rush deck.

> action predator ease up on you becasue you were back bleeding him? Was he weak
> and soft? Any self respecting Rush deck that gets provoked like that should
> have _demolished_ you. Sure, you can get his dander in an uproar by back
> bleeding him a couple times, but if you were playing a combat defense free S+B
> deck, you should have never taken an action again (as every vampire you get is
> immediately destroyed before it takes a single action) after pulling such a
> feat. What am I missing?
>

> Peter D Bakija
> PD...@aol.com
>
> "You're lucky to even know me.
> You're lucky to be alive."
> -Liz Phair

Hey Pete.

Let me try and clarify. After direct bleeding him for a handful, he got
the point that I wouldn't go quietly. His rushers were medium cap
vamps, so he only had 3 out. Plus his predator was using a presence
bleed deck to threaten him with. I guess he didn't want a fight on 2
fronts. There were 8 people playing so a quick victory wouldn't really
benefit him while everyone else was growing in power. If he fought a
war of attrition, he'd probably take me out, but then he'd be wide open
for a quick dismissmal as well.

Specifically what I did do was turtle. I had no combat capabilities
whatsoever. However, I had to make him think I was dangerous enough to
bleed him for several before I was eliminated. After he torped one and
knocked 2 others down to one, I bled him as stated. He got the point,
but I realized if I kept going over there I wouldn't last long anyway.
So I kept myself tapped taking seemingly harmless actions like hunting
and burning the pulled fangs. He had no intercept to stop me. But the
most important thing - he saw I had no blockers so he just came over to
bleed for 1-2 a turn instead of putting my remaining vamps out of their
misery. Besides he was more concerned with his predator now. He
figured I was finished and I would only punish him with more bleeds if
he angered me further.

But the real turning point came when my now-powerful prey starting
politiking. He voted to steal my predator's hunting ground card as it
was the only location available for his DisTer. This action angered my
predator into rushing his voters. Too late did he realize his error.

Now fighting a war on three fronts, he was spread too thin. A bounced
bleed from his predator took him out. I immediately influenced the 3
vamps I had waiting with 90% of their blood already on them (I hadn't
brought out anymore vamps as I knew my rushing predator would just torp
them and I'd essentially do his bleeding for him).

From the ashes of torpor Yorik rose. I eliminated my prey, the voter.
A famed vamp in torpor helped me to simultaneously eliminate my new prey
and predator with a direct bleed in both directions. In the end, I
finished in second. In good part to being able to direct bleed two
predators.

Badger

In the meantime, I influenced more vamps into my uncontrolled region -
putting enough blood on them to

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <35E1E740...@id4.telecom.fedex.com>,
Christopher Chew <c...@id4.telecom.fedex.com> wrote:

> Jyhad should not be degenerated into a situation where the only people you
>affect are you're predator and your prey.

Um, that's how the game was designed. Main foci of attention are predator
and prey, with small, mainly political interaction with other Methuselahs.

It curtails kingmaker effects (kill the person that's ahead) and *creates*
the depth and variety that isn't found in other games.

>The magic mentality of I'm going to max/mini my deck to the point of total
>predictablity, narrow focus and short game play with my competitor having no
>chance of survival is absolutely moronic. Alright 1 round Jyhad kills yea how
>great. Develop a theme yes, build in a "degree" of predictability and play the
>game (don't buy as many rare cards as you can just to assure a quick win).

Rare cards don't really figure into a strong deck, modulo Immortal Grapple --
and Potence/Foo decks have non-IG ways of coping (Psyche, Hidden Lurker,
Fast Reaction, Thoughts Betrayed -- none rare).

Giving your competitor as little chance of survival as possible is playing
to win. If you don't play to win, you're playing a much different game
than the rest of us.

There *are* no one-round-kills in Jyhad. Even with focused decks playing
to win, a 5-player table takes 90 to 150 minutes to play. Are 3 and 4
hour games superior to 1.5 to 2.5 hour games, simply by virtue of their
added length?

>Try
>bulding combat decks without IG or bums rush.

Quite possible -- Gangrel with Dogpack does quite nicely (Dogpacks and
a poolgain support system to make them affordable takes about as much
cardspace as IG in a Potence deck) with Scorpion Stings. A light
intercept deck can get a lot of mileage out of Haven Uncovered.
Imperial Decree/Covenant of Blood can be strong in the right deck.
And there is, of course, Ambush.

>Try building a prescence deck
>without majesty. Christ people develop some originality. (Note: If this last
>statement applies to you you know who you are, if not my apologies for stating
>the obvious).

Catatonic Fear and Staredown replace Majesty nicely. Celerity and Auspex
provide decent defence for the Toreador, and Thoughts Betrayed is actually
a decent combat defence for Dominate clans.

>BTW who really cares about VPs, the man still seated at the table with his
>toys still alive wins the day.

Okay. So you're playing with an entirely different set of victory conditions,
then -- essentially, in your playgroup the last methuselah standing wins
rather than (per the rules) the one with the most victory points.

Hell, no wonder you're in favor of ct bleeds -- your game dynamic is
skewed so seriously away from what the rest of us are discussing there's
no essential commonality. We're playing two different games with the
same cards.

Given that, there's really nothing further to discuss. Feel free to
play your variant as much as you wish.

gomi

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <35E1EB02...@infomatch.com>,

Karl and Sam <in...@infomatch.com> wrote:

>Good trick but unfortunately I do not think you can Cryptic Rider a Malk
>Rider Clause, for the same reason you cannot chain Cryptics together (ie.
>vote,
>CR, CR, CR etc.) Since the voting process is skipped when either CR or MRC are
>used you are not eligible to play them again after the first is used. LSJ and
>Others care to comment???

Well, the Sabbat text goes:

Cryptic Rider
Action modifier
Cost: 1 blood
Requires a ready vampire. Only usable after a successful vote. The next vote
you successfully call this turn passes automatically.

It doesn't say 'only usable during a political action' (cards with such
text cannot be played during a CR'd vote), and a CR'd vote is, ipso facto,
a successful vote, hence meets all the conditions for playing CR.

I think it's perfectly legal, given that there are no rulings prohibiting
it on the Rulemonger site.

gomi

Messages.Author: the_a...@hotmail.com
Messages.Body:
> Kevin Kelly <kke...@atlantic.net> wrote:
> > James Coupe wrote:
> >
> > In article <35E0412B...@buffnet.net>, badger <bad...@buffnet.net>
> > writes
> > >Why?
> > >
> > >Rush/combat decks can target anyone they want. Political decks can
> > >target anyone they want. To some extent, you can intercept anyone you
> > >want (Eagle Sight, Anneke, etc). Therefore, I should be able to bleed
> > >ANYONE I want to. Why is bleeding being handicapped?
> >
> > Rush/combat incapacitates a minion, not pool.
>
> This is a weak argument that everyone keeps throwing around. Why is a
> minion considered less than pool.

A number of reasons, primarily that losing a minion _cannot_ directly oust
you, whereas loosing pool can. Look back in the threads for a discussion of
primary and secondary resources.

>Number one, you must use pool to get a minion.

Yes, and that minion may take actions to refill itself. In a way, a minion is
a self perpetuating resource, whereas pool is _difficult_ to replace. It
requires a sequence of cards, and is often easily disrupted (blocking the
5th, torporing the blood doll, burning the powerbase).

> Second, I usually have ways to get pool from minions so
> losing a minion with blood is just like losing pool in the amount of
> blood on them.

Are you sure? this seems a little confused: losing blood on minions is
_nothing_ like losing pool. If anything, blood on minions (along with
counters on cards, etc) is a tertiary resource, and even more easy to replace
than the first two, In fact, there is a base level action (hunting) that
directly replaces some of this resource. There is no such thing for secondary
resources (vamps, etc) or primary resource (pool).

> Third, you can more easily do large amounts of blood
> damage in combat than you can in bleed damage to pool.

How is this an argument _for_ CTB? I must be missing your point.

> Finally, many times I would *rather* lose pool than minions (depending on the
> minion) because the loss of that minion could criple me.

BUT: if it was a choice of losing pool (and being ousted) or losing a minion,
you can (should) see that losing a minion is _not_ as direct a factor to
ousting as is being bled.

>
> > Political affects pool but EVERYONE can vote.
>
> Everyone with a political deck or that happens to have titled vampires.

However, titled vampires are relatively common, and vote gaining reaction
cards/ vote effecting cards are plentiful, and skill-less. Even non political
decks can usually swing a vote or three, and a table full of votes must be
overcome before any particular voting action can be successful. Contrast this
to the lack of bleed defense available, particularly skill-less or innate.

>
> > Intercept is not pro-active. People can get round intercept
> > (unblockability, actions that don't care if they're blocked - combat
> > etc.). Intercept can only affect minions, not pool.
>
> You can't get around intercept any easier than you can avoid being bled
> (intercept, bleed bounce, killing the bleeders). Some decks can't have
> a very hard time getting around intercept, some decks have a hard time
> avioding bleeds there isn't much difference. See above for affecting
> minions.

Yes you can. Intercept offers the opportunity to pound the miscreant into the
turf, and otherwise explain rather forcefully why they shouldn't do this ;)

Seriously though, Intercept _at not point_ can cause you to loose pool.
Intercept is _defensive_. Bleeding is aggressive, and particularly CTB,
directly targets that which keeps you in the game.

>
> > Bleed affects pool and only one person can stop it. If it goes cross-
> > table, still only one person can stop it - and not a person who was
> > expecting to get hit by you.
>
> Just like you weren't expecting to get hit by an arson, or a rush, or
> .... I say just learn to expect it. Besides I am always concerned
> about bleeds since that is the name of the game (whoever they are from).

No, the name of the game is ousting your prey. Beyond this, any of the other
actions you name may _indirectly_ contribute to your ousting (other actions to
reduce your pool are still required), but Bleed directly expedites your exit.

>
> > *sigh*
> >
> > Bleed: gets rid of pool (unlike combat)
>
> One is not worse than the other

Definitely disagree here. Do you _really_ believe that combat (and having
minions incapacitated) is as bad as losing the game?

>
> > doesn't interact with whole table (unlike vote)
>
> Most people at the table can't affect a vote anyway.

Not even nearly true. Sudden reaction, Pulling Strings, Innate titles,
delaying tactics, all these cards and effects make it easy to play the
politics game. If you fail to include them, that is a choice. BUT: anti-bleed
cards such as deflection, reduction and intercept are discipline specific,
and cannot be included in many decks.

>
> >
> > So: it can only affect your prey.
>
> Which is just plain wrong.
>

No it is not. Bleeding as a cardless action can only effect your prey. Why
should carded bleeding, which bestows other advantages (such as increased
bleed) be at all different?

>Don't you get it ........ there is no limit to the reasoning for performing ct
>actions,

No, no, no. You misunderstand completely. If we didn't see the need
for ANY cross-table interaction, we'd be arguing that Rushes should be
only playable on your predator/prey, that votes should only target them
etc. But a bleed is just too easy and powerful to pull off.

Losing a minion to torpor is painful. But they can be rescued. Losing
a minion to burning is also painful, but it's not the same as losing
pool - if I had three minions out for 15 pool, and had 15 pool left,
losing a minion means I still have 15 pool left, whereas losing pool
means I have less than 15 pool left. With a minion gone, I can use that
15 pool as I choose. With less pool, it's a harder tougher choice.

Voting can get rid of pool, yes, but bleed is just VERY easy to do. It
shouldn't be thrown about willy-nilly. Combat is difficult and only
gets rid of blood which can be got back with Fifth Tradition, Hunting,
Aaron's, IDF, Giant's Blood, Festivo dello Estinto, Hunting Grounds,
Taste of Vitae, Steal blood and so forth. Pool is much harder to get
back.

>The magic mentality of I'm going to max/mini my deck to the point of total
>predictablity, narrow focus and short game play with my competitor having no
>chance of survival is absolutely moronic.

No, not at all. This is something I fail to see the point of. I *can*
build a very wide deck, but if I want to build a narrow deck, why not?
I fail to see how a narrow deck is not fun. It seems to be a school of
thought that just because I draw similar cards a lot of the time that a
deck must be not fun and the player must be moronic? Why? It is quite
possible to have a lot of fun with a fairly pure rush deck. I know,
I've built them before. I'm not a good player of them, but it was a
bloody fun deck and got quite a few remarks about it.

Being reliable in what I draw isn't the same as being boring.

>Alright 1 round Jyhad kills yea how
>great. Develop a theme yes, build in a "degree" of predictability and play the

>game (don't buy as many rare cards as you can just to assure a quick win). Try

>bulding combat decks without IG or bums rush.

Building combat decks without some form of rush is facile. I need to be
able to get into combat and not have to rely on blocking. The only
other way to do it would be to do intercept, but that requires my
predator/prey to attempt blockable actions. Haven Uncovered, Ambush,
Contract and Archon are all usable and used alternatives.

From the IG point of view, it's difficult. One combat tactic is to
include either Dodge or S:CE in a non-combat deck. IG is one of the
only reliable ways. Thoughts Betrayed and Dog Pack also work, and the
ability to restart combats are also possible. However, Potence has some
advantages of its own in that it's fairly easy to do big hits, whereas
Gangrel find it harder to hit big and burn you - torporisation is fairly
easy, but they can't carry a blood hunt vote :( And the Tremere
normally have to wait till second round for the good strikes. It's an
unfortunate fact that it's just difficult to pull off another form of
combat.

> Try building a prescence deck
>without majesty. Christ people develop some originality. (Note: If this last
>statement applies to you you know who you are, if not my apologies for stating
>the obvious).
>

Why use Majesty when you can use Catatonic Fear? <evil grin>
Actually, I don't like Majesty that much anyway. I throw maybe a couple
in as a little defence, but not too many.

>-Chris

>
>BTW who really cares about VPs, the man still seated at the table with his
>toys still alive wins the day.

Not at all. The last man standing doesn't always win. The guy with
most VPs does, which isn't necessarily the same thing.

Offense, yes. Blind attack, no.

> from profiting when they snipe c-t bleeds. The problem isn't in the advantages

>
> Here's where I used to agree with you. The thing is, if you do something
> that doesn't help you, but ousts me, the game is not at all fun for me. If I
> am sitting merrily at 8 pool and have destroyed all of my predator's
> vampires, I usually don't have anything to worry about. If my deck is pretty
> strong, then I should probably win. If you are my grand-predator, however,
> and you decide to bleed me for 8 with a GtU + action modifiers and stuff,
> then I get ousted, and your prey gains 6 pool and a VP. That didn't help you
> at all. All it did was screw me over. And why would you do this? Maybe
> you're just an all-around jerk. Maybe you don't really know how to play the
> game. Maybe I accidentally bumped into you before the tournament and you're
> pissed off at me. I don't know. All I know is, when people do things that
> hurt you and don't help them, the game is not fun. (BTW, when I say "you" I
> don't mean you personally, but some people actually play the game this way.
> If we were to ban these people, then I would be back to being in favour of
> ct-bleeds.)

I think I now understand why I don't understand. I have played in only
one tournament (which I hated beyond belief). Every other time I've
played it has been with friends and friends of friends. I almost never
had to deal with truely random play. Sometimes people would do things
that didn't benefit them only because they *thought* it would but
didn't. Usually they saw the error of their ways and didn't try that
again, so we saw things like this very infrequently. If someone did
start to exibit random behavior because "they thought it was funny", we
would always gang up on them or guilt them out of not acting like a
horses rear end. Since we regularly played with the same groups, this
usually worked (wouldn't probably do squat at a tourny though). I also
can see if I geared up to play a tournament, hoping to win, built what I
think is a very good deck. The deck works wonderful and out of nowhere
someone bleeds me for no reason and ruins my whole game - yes I can see
how this could be frustrating. Now if I was any reason for them doing it
them I should have been prepared and if I wasn't then, well, you snooze
you lose. But if it was a totally random act then yes, that wouldn't be
fun.

So I guess I concede, for tournament play, there probably needs to be a
little more predictability (Jyhad has always been a pretty unpredictable
game). I don't think I will ever ban c-t bleeds in play with friends
though because with friends, I don't care as much (we'll play again soon
anyway) and I'd hate to diminish any stratagy (because to keep it fresh
you have to constantly do new things). I do think c-t bleeds have a
place in Jyhad, maybe it just isn't in tournaments.

Kevin

PS. Are there people out there who think that c-t bleeds are bad even
without the random factor (ie. Someone bleeding c-t when it doesn't help
them)?

Messages.Body:
Kevin Kelly (kke...@atlantic.net) wrote:
: PDB6 wrote:
: >
: > invariably strengthens your enemies (the people sitting next to you).
: > Voting
: > to hurt someone across the table is dumb. Rushing someone across the
: > table is
: > dumb. Bleeding someone across the table is dumb. It strengthens your
: > enemies,
: > wastes your actions, and weakens your position. Never a good idea.

: Never is an awful strong word. I agree that it is *usually* not a good

: idea take cross-table actions. This statement alone makes me wonder why
: people are so adament about eliminating them. By eliminating something
: which you have said never helps (I disagree with never) you also stop me

: from including something that I think *may* help. I you don't think it
: helps me, WHY DO YOU CARE. I'm saying that sometimes it does help and
: I may just want to prepare appropriately for that situation. It is up
: to the skill of a player to determine when it is good (seldom) and when
: it is detrimental. Don't tell me I can't do it just because *you* don't
: think it can help me. (This goes for all forms of cross table actions
: not just bleeds - I have used them all at one time or another at a
: definate help to me).

What's never a good idea is the 'strengthening your enemies, wasting
your actions, and weakening your position.' I recognize that a cross-
table-bleed at the right time can win you the game. It shouldn't
be able to. There should be no kingmaking in Jyhad. It is a game
*involving* diplomacy, but it is not Diplomacy.

It's not that I don't think it can help you. I think it can help
you in certain situations. In those situations you shouldn't be
allowed to do it because it's too powerful. In the situations when
it won't help you, you shouldn't be allowed to do it because you'd
be shooting yourself in the foot. ;-)

: > Anything that comprimises
: > good design weakens the game.

: I agree, so why take out ct-bleeds?

Because they reduce the amount of in-game strategy and increase the
amount of politics. [relative to the original state of the game before
CT bleeds were introduced by the old rules team]

Josh

Messages.Author: Kevin Kelly
Messages.Body:
the_a...@hotmail.com wrote:
>
> A number of reasons, primarily that losing a minion _cannot_ directly oust
> you, whereas loosing pool can. Look back in the threads for a discussion of
> primary and secondary resources.

Your making the assumption that every c-t bleed will oust.

> >Number one, you must use pool to get a minion.
>
> Yes, and that minion may take actions to refill itself. In a way, a minion is
> a self perpetuating resource, whereas pool is _difficult_ to replace. It
> requires a sequence of cards, and is often easily disrupted (blocking the
> 5th, torporing the blood doll, burning the powerbase).

A minion is only self perpetuating if it is alive. This same self
perpetuation is also the primary way to get pool (ie. pull it off the
vampire). If the vampire is dead you just lost the minion *and* a
possible source of pool.

> Are you sure? this seems a little confused: losing blood on minions is
> _nothing_ like losing pool. If anything, blood on minions (along with
> counters on cards, etc) is a tertiary resource, and even more easy to replace
> than the first two, In fact, there is a base level action (hunting) that
> directly replaces some of this resource. There is no such thing for secondary
> resources (vamps, etc) or primary resource (pool).

This is true of course. Blood on minions is not directly as important
as pool. However, it is rather easy to do massive damage whereas it is
not as easy to do massive bleeds. This blood on the vampire is not
directly as important as pool but there are many ways to make it become
pool, but only if you have excess blood to begin with.

> > Third, you can more easily do large amounts of blood
> > damage in combat than you can in bleed damage to pool.
>
> How is this an argument _for_ CTB? I must be missing your point.

Very indirectly at this point. People are claiming that c-t bleeds are
"bad" and c-t rush is not. This is claimed because they say that
minions ar not as important as pool. I disagree and am attempting to
show why I consider them of equal importance (depending on *many* game
time situations). I am saying that it is not to terribly difficult to
hit my 8 cap vamp for 9 - send him to torpor with no blood and I now am
missing 8 blood that I probably paid for with 8 pool. It is much more
difficult to bleed for 8. No, they are not directly relatable - an 8
bleed in much worse than being hit for 8. But They are both very
detrimental and I am simply pointing out that I consider minion loss
equal to pool loss in general.

>
> > Finally, many times I would *rather* lose pool than minions (depending on the
> > minion) because the loss of that minion could criple me.
>
> BUT: if it was a choice of losing pool (and being ousted) or losing a minion,
> you can (should) see that losing a minion is _not_ as direct a factor to
> ousting as is being bled.

Again, you are assuming that if I am losing pool I am being ousted. Of
course being ousted is the worst. But assume I have 6 blood. If I have
the choice of being bleed for 3 or losing my last vampire I will lose
the blood. At this point I am in poor shape one way or the other but
with a vampire up I at least may have a shot at recovery. If pool was
so much more important why would I ever influence a vampire to begin
with - which obviously makes no sense.

> >
> > > Political affects pool but EVERYONE can vote.
> >
> > Everyone with a political deck or that happens to have titled vampires.
>
> However, titled vampires are relatively common, and vote gaining reaction
> cards/ vote effecting cards are plentiful, and skill-less. Even non political
> decks can usually swing a vote or three, and a table full of votes must be
> overcome before any particular voting action can be successful. Contrast this
> to the lack of bleed defense available, particularly skill-less or innate.

Apearently my experiences are different that yours. Usually, the only
thing that can stop a powerful vote deck is anouther vote deck. Vote
reaction cards are almost unheard of in my play circles.

> >
> > > Intercept is not pro-active. People can get round intercept
> > > (unblockability, actions that don't care if they're blocked - combat
> > > etc.). Intercept can only affect minions, not pool.
> >
> > You can't get around intercept any easier than you can avoid being bled
> > (intercept, bleed bounce, killing the bleeders). Some decks can't have
> > a very hard time getting around intercept, some decks have a hard time
> > avioding bleeds there isn't much difference. See above for affecting
> > minions.
>
> Yes you can. Intercept offers the opportunity to pound the miscreant into the
> turf, and otherwise explain rather forcefully why they shouldn't do this ;)
>
> Seriously though, Intercept _at not point_ can cause you to loose pool.
> Intercept is _defensive_. Bleeding is aggressive, and particularly CTB,
> directly targets that which keeps you in the game.

I don't understand this point, could you reexplain it. I think the
original point was that intercept can also affect other meths, James
gave reasons why this wasn't as important and I countered.

> >

> > Besides I am always concerned
> > about bleeds since that is the name of the game (whoever they are from).
>
> No, the name of the game is ousting your prey. Beyond this, any of the other
> actions you name may _indirectly_ contribute to your ousting (other actions to
> reduce your pool are still required), but Bleed directly expedites your exit.

You're right. What I meant to say was that I am usually ready to block
a bleed (intending from my pred but could be from anywhere). It's true
though that some decks really have no blocking capabiltiy (esp rush
decks) and are much more vulnerable to c-t bleeds (although much less
vulnerable to c-t rush).

> Definitely disagree here. Do you _really_ believe that combat (and having
> minions incapacitated) is as bad as losing the game?

You keep assuming that you'll get ousted on every c-t bleed. This was
not my assumption and I understand your confusion if you thought it was.

> >
> > > doesn't interact with whole table (unlike vote)
> >
> > Most people at the table can't affect a vote anyway.
>
> Not even nearly true. Sudden reaction, Pulling Strings, Innate titles,
> delaying tactics, all these cards and effects make it easy to play the
> politics game. If you fail to include them, that is a choice. BUT: anti-bleed
> cards such as deflection, reduction and intercept are discipline specific,
> and cannot be included in many decks.

Again, this is just different from my experience where the reaction vote
cards are seldom used.

> >
> > >
> > > So: it can only affect your prey.
> >
> > Which is just plain wrong.
> >
>
> No it is not. Bleeding as a cardless action can only effect your prey. Why
> should carded bleeding, which bestows other advantages (such as increased
> bleed) be at all different?

Yes, as a cardless action you can only bleed your prey, I would never
disagree with that. Having to use cards for the action I think puts the
correct level of restriction. Carded bleedsing means that you must
design your deck to effectivly be able to bleed anywhere and this really
doesn't pay off. Therefore c-t bleeds are an occational tool you can
use to help your situation (I am disregarding random c-t bleeds which I
agree are anoying).

Kevin

all the years I have played I have only used this tool maybe 4 times total
so removing it will cause very little change. At least around here.

If you CT bleed regularly you can't win (0 VP's = loss) It is however
a tool you can use to buy time and help yourself win occasionally.
The main arguments I've heard on the subject point to this supposed
renegade player who does it out of spite and or ignorance, But I feel
this renegade will figure out quite quickly that they can't win like that
and will change the behavior on their own.
Richard Garfield put it this way: (quoted from the original Jyhad players
guide)
" If a player is inclined to remove someone other than their prey then
she is either gaining some advantage from the move, hence being
rewarded, or she should reconsider her strategy."
This says to me that the designer realized that a good player can and
should be able to oust someone other than their prey "IF" it helps them.

Was this really a problem ????

suggests that the best thing to play is a super-defensive intercept
deck.
