Kevin Kelly <kke...@atlantic.net> wrote:

> Who here counts victory points at the end of a game outside of a
> tournament?

We do. Every group I've played with (4 people for a year, 20 people
for a year, 6 people for 1.5 years, and 4 people for a year) has. It's the
only real way to say who wins as that's what is defined by the rulebook.
As someone else already stated, it's an entirely different game if you
take out this element. If your group uses the house rule that last person
standing is the winner and all you wanted to do is win, then why not play
bounce/intercept and blood gain every game? I sure would unless I
made a deck to toy with everyone else.

> For those who do, is it considered more important in you play group to
> be the last at the table or the one with the most VPs?

Being last man standing gives nothing more than minor satisfaction at
having ousted someone who may have gained 6 or more pool from ousting
other people. The point of the game is ousting your prey. If you only
do it once while someone else does it twice, why should you be considered
the winner?

Mike

>
> This brings up a very intersting question.
>

> Who here counts victory points at the end of a game outside of a
> tournament?
>

> For those who do, is it considered more important in you play group to

> be the last at the table or the one with the most VPs?
>

Everyone I've ever played with counts victory points. This includes a
playgroup of about 5 people in the Chicago area, about 15 people in Pasadena,
and all Jyhad On-Line games (which may become the future of the game if this
new expansion thingie doesn't pan out).

The fact is, being the last one standing doesn't necessarily mean anything.
If you have an intercept deck that does nothing but block, you will almost
certainly be the last one standing. However, you prey who just ousted 3
people and runs out of cards and concedes will (or at least should!) have a
problem with you claiming total victory.

Allowing the last person left to win the game encourages passive play, and
results in 3 hour (or longer) games that are not exciting at any point.
Using Victory Points (as per even the most basic rules of the game), however,
ensures that people must try to *do* something in order to win. With
everyone trying to oust his or her prey as quickly as possible to rack up
VP's, the game goes faster and usually has some pretty exciting parts.

Kevin Kelly (kke...@atlantic.net) wrote:

: This is true of course. Blood on minions is not directly as important

I think it's inaccurate to say that it's 'easy' to do massive damage
to a vampire compared to doing a massive bleed. I'm not sure in what
sense you're using the word 'easy', but the combination of cards
needed for a large bleed is smaller than that needed for a high-
damage successful combat.

Compare:

Bum's Rush, Torn Signpost, Fists of Death, Undead Strength: 4-7
damage depending on inferior/superior potence; 4 cards.

Govern the Unaligned, Conditioning: 5-6 bleed depending on inferior/
superior dominate; 2 cards.

That's assuming a victim with no countermeasures. For the combat deck,
if they have damage prevention or strike: combat ends or dodge, you
need to add Immortal Grapple and maybe some presses. For the bleed
deck, if they have intercept, you need to add a stealth card.

: Very indirectly at this point. People are claiming that c-t bleeds are

: "bad" and c-t rush is not. This is claimed because they say that
: minions ar not as important as pool. I disagree and am attempting to
: show why I consider them of equal importance (depending on *many* game
: time situations). I am saying that it is not to terribly difficult to
: hit my 8 cap vamp for 9 - send him to torpor with no blood and I now am
: missing 8 blood that I probably paid for with 8 pool. It is much more
: difficult to bleed for 8. No, they are not directly relatable - an 8
: bleed in much worse than being hit for 8. But They are both very
: detrimental and I am simply pointing out that I consider minion loss
: equal to pool loss in general.

To hit your 8 camp vamp for 9, I need to have the right cards at the
right time, and I need you to not have a Skin of Steel.

(Bum's Rush, Torn Signpost, Immortal Grapple, Blur: 9 damage if I
have both superior Celerity and Potence. This is the 'easiest' way to
get 9 damage I know of, and it needs two superior disciplines.)

To bleed for 8 in a single action is 'difficult'; the easiest way
off the top of my head would be an IC member bleeding with Govern the
Unaligned and Conditioning (8 bleed, 2 cards). To bleed for 8
in two actions is 'easy'; the most straightforward way is two
vamps with dom each using a Govern and a Bonding (8 bleed, 4 cards).

Losing a vampire to torpor is bad. But in the midgame, losing that
vampire's capacity in pool is generally much worse.

Josh

I'm confused as your statements are pretty contradictory on face value.

In article <35E2C45B...@atlantic.net>,
Kevin Kelly <kke...@atlantic.net> wrote:

First apparent contradiction,
----
> This blood on the vampire is not directly as important as pool,

> but there are many ways to make it become
> pool, but only if you have excess blood to begin with.

and later

> [ct-bleeds being bad and ct-rush being ok] is claimed because they say that

> minions ar not as important as pool. I disagree and am attempting to
> show why I consider them of equal importance (depending on *many* game
> time situations).

----

In the first statement, you say that vampire blood is not
directly as important as pool. In other words, unless you have
the cards to bring the vampire's blood back to your pool, they
are definitely not as important. In the second statement,
you say they are of equal importance. Hrmmm, now that I'm re-reading
this, I think I may of mininterpreted your "depending on many game
time situations" qualifier.

So if it's only as important in cases where you are trying to get
the blood back, then vampire blood's importance depends on your
metagame, ie. how many Blood Dolls, Minion Taps people use or combat
efficiency.

Second apparent contradiction in consecutive sentences
----
> No, [bleeding for 8 and a vampire taking 8 damage] are not directly

> relatable - an 8 bleed in much worse than being hit for 8. But They are
> both very detrimental and I am simply pointing out that I consider minion loss
> equal to pool loss in general.

----

First you say that a bleed of 8 is much worse than a vampire getting
hit for 8, but then you say you consider them equal. Why?

Look at it this way. Let's say there is this card:

Sock it to Ya!
Master
Your prey must either burn 8 pool or one of your prey's vampires
takes 8 damage.

I can tell you that 99% of the time, I would take the 8 damage on
my vampire rather than the pool. The only time I would take the
pool burn is if I can definitely kill my prey with that vampire during
my turn, assuming I have the blood to take the 8 point pool burn.

> I am saying that it is not to terribly difficult to
> hit my 8 cap vamp for 9 - send him to torpor with no blood and I now am
> missing 8 blood that I probably paid for with 8 pool. It is much more
> difficult to bleed for 8.

This is a metagame issue. In my group, hitting a vampire for 9
is VERY difficult to do. There's a very good balance of combat
defense. If you manage to damage a vampire for 9 (in any number of
strikes in one round of combat), you got pretty lucky. However,
having a bleed for 8 is not super incredibly difficult to accomplish.
The only thing that stops bleeds this size in our group is fear of Archon
Investigation.

Mike

The fact that it doesn't restrict who you may bleed.

Computer Hacking says nothing about only bleeding your prey, so you may bleed
anyone. Neither your argument nor mine is convincing. I think you know that.

If I were to say, "Hit someone," you would have no idea as to who you must
hit. If you hit the person on your right, and I said, "you're not allowed to
do that, I told you to hit the person on your left," you would think I was
nuts.

The broadest I will go is to compare it to saying "Attack." Well, in this
case, I'm not sure who to attack. You didn't say that I must attack the
person on my left, so it is logical to assume that I can attack the person on
my right if I wish. Your argument says something to the effect of "without
instruction, you may attack the person on your left." Well, great, but I
have an instruction. That instruction is "Attack." So why can't I attack
anyone I want? The "attack" instruction is ambiguous.

clarification as to who a carded bleed may target. Since I can vaguely see

agree, however, with people arguing that this was "obviously" the original
intent. When I first heard that (D)bleeds could target any methuselah, I

originally played the other way, but either way makes sense from the original
rules.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Kevin Kelly wrote:
"For those who do, is it considered more important in you play group to be the
last at the table or the one with the most VPs?"

The game's victory conditions are Victory Points. If the game ends with me
ousted, but with 3 VPs and one other guy at the table, still alive with 2 VPs,
I still win. Granted, in most situations this makes not a stitch of
difference, but then neither does winning in any game.

If you are playing a game, then winning is, at some level, important. if not,
you might as well be doing something else. Role Playing comes to mind,
initially, but then so does going down to a pub for a pint. People generally
play games because they enjoy the puzzle solving involved, and the ultimate
expression of solving the puzzles correctly is winning.

Sure, I don't _really_ care if I win a game of Jyhad, but it is always nice to
win occasionally. As the victory conditions are "Get the most Victory Points",
then that is what is used to gauge said victory. Yes, being the last guy alive
at the table is always good for sort of a moral victory, but it is still the
guy with the most VPs who wins, alive or not.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 25 Aug 1998, Kevin Kelly wrote:

> Who here counts victory points at the end of a game outside of a
> tournament?

I do. This is expecially true since I am trying to evaluate my own decks
as I play them. Winning 2 victory points is a very respectable showing
even if someone else gets 3. There is a big difference between being
ousted with one victory point and being ousted with none.

I have always counted the relative degrees of victory. I'm sure this is
true of most people. This is, after all a multi-player game that is
generally thought best with about 5 players. If you view it as strictly
"either I win, or I lose", then it will be rather discouraging, as the
average player will "lose" about 80% of the time, after devoting two or
more hours to a typical game.

> For those who do, is it considered more important in you play group to >
> be the last at the table or the one with the most VPs?

Usually the last person standing *is* the person with the most VPs. In
the rare instances where this is not the case, my playgroup certainly
consideres the deck with the most VPs as having won top honors.

Imagine player A ousts 3 opponents, then successfully withdraws leaving
player B the last standing. Player A has 4 victory points, and player B
has 1. I doubt that anyone would have trouble with the idea that player A
has made the best showing.

I will not deny that that one victory point you get for being the last
standing has a slightly higher luster than any other victory point. Thus,
if you had a "tie game" where player A was the last standing with 2
victory points, after ousting player B with 2 victory points, then player
A is usually just a little more satisfied with himself. But that never
stops player B from pointing out that it is, in fact, a tie.

In article <6rusvk$gsl$1...@nnrp1.dejanews.com>, <ber...@cco.caltech.edu> wrote:

>Eh? Don't take that bullshit. People can argue until they're blue in the

>face about "original intent." However, it is not clear at all that ct-bleeds
>were not originally intended. At best, the original rules are ambiguous on
>the issue.

Actually, it's quite evident, as a simple perusal of the rulebook shows:

(from 6.4, 'Minion Actions'):

"Bleed (no card required): Bleeding is one of the most fundamental directed
actions in the game. A minion controlled by a Methuselah attempts to reduce
the blood pool of another Methuselah. [...]

1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your minion is attempting
to bleed.
2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful in their
attempts to stop you, your prey burns one pool. There are also cards that
allow your minions to bleed your prey for more than one pool."

I encourage you to note the word 'prey' used throughout in the definition
of 'bleed.'

Since 'bleed' definitionally includes a prey-only restriction, specific
cardtext is required for a bleed card to affect a non-prey methuselah.

There isn't any ambiguity at all.

gomi

The rules restrict whom you can bleed. The fact that the card doesn't

your Prey.

> bleeding your prey that the rules mention when defining the default bleed

The card says "bleed". It doesn't reiterate all the rules about bleeding,
since it doesn't have to. For instance, the bit about getting the Edge if
you are successful (1 or more) isn't changed by using a cardless vs. carded
bleed. And neither is the bit about the bleed being directed at your Prey.
The only thing that is changed by (for instance) Computer Hacking is the
amount of the bleed, because card text explicitly changes the amount.

> > OK. So you can use Cat Burglary, Night Moves, and Kindred Spirits to
> > bleed someone other than your Prey because card text says so.
> >
> > But Computer Hacking says nothing about being able to bleed someone
> > other than your prey, so you have to bleed your prey.
> >
> Computer Hacking says nothing about only bleeding your prey, so you may bleed
> anyone.

It says "bleed". That means "prey" since the rules say so.

> Neither your argument nor mine is convincing. I think you know that.

I know you are not convinced by my argument and that I am not convinced
by yours, yes. But that doesn't mean that one of the arguments is not
convincing.

> If I were to say, "Hit someone," you would have no idea as to who you must
> hit. If you hit the person on your right, and I said, "you're not allowed to
> do that, I told you to hit the person on your left," you would think I was

Right. Unless the definition of "hit" included the stipulation it was an
activity that is directed at the person on your left by default.

> The broadest I will go is to compare it to saying "Attack." Well, in this
> case, I'm not sure who to attack. You didn't say that I must attack the
> person on my left, so it is logical to assume that I can attack the person on
> my right if I wish.

Right, unless the rules have provided a stipulation on who is the target
of an "attack".

> Your argument says something to the effect of "without
> instruction, you may attack the person on your left."

But you have instruction - the rules.

My argument is better stated as:
"In the absence of overriding instruction, the rules apply"
(implication of the Golden Rule for Cards, sec. 12).

> Well, great, but I
> have an instruction. That instruction is "Attack." So why can't I attack
> anyone I want? The "attack" instruction is ambiguous.

For "Attack", sure.

For "bleed", no. The rulebook is clear that this action is directed
against the player's Prey. The ambiguity arises only when the rules are
ignored.

: think that the restriction that you need a card to do it, along with the
: fact that it is usually not a benefit to the person doing it is more
: that enough to it's power on equal grounds with other actions which

The restriction of 'you need a card to CT-bleed' amounts to (as far
as I can see) 'you need to be playing a bleed deck.' Any bleed deck
I've seen someone play has had enough (D) bleed cards in it that they
could make every bleed a CT-bleed if they wanted to. In other words,
it's not a restriction at all, since the only decks that can usefully
CT-bleed already have the cards they would need to do it.

Even though it's usually not going to be worthwhile to CT-bleed someone,
that doesn't make it any less powerful when it *is* useful. If a
game goes along for twenty turns, and the person across the table has
just picked up a VP, and looks like they're about to get another (but
they're currently low on pool), and you oust them with a CT-bleed,
that is much more powerful than calling a vote which everyone else
on the table is allowed to influence, or Bum's Rushing one of their
vampires.

: You state "relative to the original state of the game before CT bleeds

: were introduced by the old rules team". I would like to know, original
: state according to whom? I have played since it came out and didn't
: know a "rules team" existed until about two years ago and I have always
: played that way and never met anyone who didn't. I think the rules team
: made it official because that's how the majority played. I have seen
: some different interpretations of the rules and they were (are?)
: ambiguous so I could really see it either way according to the original
: book.

There has been a 'rules team' ever since the game was invented; the
people on it decided on the proper interpretation of the rules and
whether changes should be made to them.

The original state of the game was that the Jyhad rulebook didn't
allow cross-table bleeds (since it was inherent in the definition of
the 'bleed' action that it was directed at your prey - the (D) symbol
was only a reminder that actions with it were directed).

Going back and looking at DejaNews posts, it seems that the Rules
Team at that time denied that their interpretation of (D) bleeds
was actually a change. On May 9, 1995, Tom Wylie (then the Netrep
for Jyhad) posted a set of Design Team Rulings including this:

"If an action card such as Computer Hacking provides a directed bleed,
you may bleed any player other than yourself. This overrides the
rules for the default bleed, which is a directed action only usable
against your prey. This is something else that changed during
playtesting, which is why Cat Burglary indicates different rules
for directed bleeds. Any future printings of Cat Burglary will
be changed to make the card useful."

This ruling set off some dispute on the newsgroup, in which some of
the sensible players argued with Tom about what the (D) symbol was
supposed to mean and whether Cat Burglary had been written correctly.

The Rules Team almost certainly made it official because that was
how they thought the rules should be, rather than based on any kind
of majority opinion they felt the players had. The Rules Team has
always seemed to feel that their job is not to reflect the will of
the masses, but what they think is right.

Do you mean Cryptic Rider? Jyhad and VTES text are clear according to

passes automatically.' (In other words, also wrong. I don't think
I've ever played this way, but it sounds familiar for some reason.)

> My argument is better stated as:

>

> against the player's Prey. The ambiguity arises only when the rules are
> ignored.

Well, for just a moment, I'll assume that's true. (The rulebook actually
says that bleeds are your way of reducing a methuselah's pool (doesn't
mention prey there), and then goes on to describe how you execute the default
cardless bleed (which *is* restricted to your prey).) So, "bleed" is defined
to be against your prey? In that case, any card which says, "(D)Bleed your
predator" would be nonsensical. If bleed by definition targets only prey,
then this whole statement is a contradiction.

Another stupid analogy... "Fishing" is defined, rather loosely, as catching
fish. If I said, "go fishing," you would know pretty much what I meant
(note: I don't care if you go fly fishing or trout fishing or whatever...
ignore that). If I instead said, "go fishing for deer," the statement does
not make sense. You might figure some way around that and decide I meant
"hunting" but that's not the same thing. There is no way to strictly
interpret my instructions such that they make sense. "Go catch fish for
deer?!?"

That said, since there *are* ways to bleed other methuselahs (including bleed
bounce, some carded bleeds, and I think a particular vampire's special
ability), it is not possible for the term "bleed" to automatically indicate
your prey. The word "bleed" is used in those circumstances to indicate the
burning of blood from another methuselah's pool. *That* it seems is the
definition of "bleed." So, a card which says "(D) Bleed" cannot carry any
more restrictions than the word "bleed" does. And if "bleed" carries the
restriction of "prey" then "(D) Bleed your predator" makes no sense.

Personally, I make myself feel better by telling myself that this new
restriction against ct-bleeds is errata to all (D) bleed cards to make them
say, "(D) Bleed your prey." That way, I can accept the ruling (which I have
grudgingly admitted is best for the game) without losing sleep at night (you
don't want to know the sort of things that keep me up at night... sad,
really).

-Chris

Actually, if you read the original rulebook on political actions, only the
_other_ Methuselahs (i.e., not the Vote Caller) could push votes.

The various interpretations from there (the original DCI all-push, the
subsequent SPTR 1 PA per PA, the next DCI delayed replenishment, and finally
the DCI's current 1 PA per PA status) are attempts to keep play fair and
balanced. The initial DCI interpretation (and an initial intuitive
interpretation) was made difficult by a shoddily worded rulebook, but the
current Vote Push rule strives for what the original wording strives for: a
balanced vote environment.

> I liked CTB, but I can certainly
> live without them. What I find odd is that deflections and the like remain
> unaltered. These reactions are tantamount to bleeds and should be dealt
> with similarly if we are so concerned with the predator-prey relation.

Can't say I see this as an argument...

The ability of a defensive deck to play a defensive card is reliant upon an
aggressor towards that strategy. A bleeder can simply use their strategy from
the get-go.

Not only is there much less opportunity for a cross-table bouncer to be
effective, it requires far to many conditionals for it to be a big deal (must
have an aggressive bleeder, must have a deflection available, must for some
reason bring it acrossed the table, must have to have aggressive bleeder
continue to supply aggressive bleeds for deflection to become problematic).

See the above arguments. (D) only limits who may block the action
- the recipient of the action as directed. In the case of a bleed, it may
be redundant (since bleeds may only ever be blocked by the prey) but
for consistency's sake (and the presence of a revised rules-set regarding
carded bleeds) the (D) was retained.

If we had a hypothetical card which read strictly

Public Assault

Choose any minion in play. Begin a combat between the acting
minion and this target.

the minion's controller _could not block_ the action, instead
the opportunity would pass to the prey, then the predator,
as per all normal actions. The absence of the (D) in the above
text indicates that normal rules concerning blocking take effect.

In the case of

(D) Bleed your predator

The first (D) is reminder text, but also present to bring some
consistency to the card set (since most actions which target
other methuselahs or their minions have the (D) symbol.)
The Bleed text 'activates' the rules set regarding bleeds,
modifying them in the targetting section - the bleed must be
targetted to your predator, instead of the prey.

Q: How does a Computer Hacking differ from a cardless bleed?
A:
1) The presence/use of a card
2) In other ways as listed on the card

Since the card doesn't say that it is changing the default behavior
of a "bleed" in terms of who the bleed can target, it follows
the default behavoir of a bleed in that regard.

Similarly, since the card doesn't say that it is changing the
default behavior of a bleed in terms of getting the Edge if
the bleed successfully resolves for one or more, it follows the
default behavior of a bleed in that regard.

And so on for: who can block, how to block (intercept/stealth),
amount of the bleed (although most bleed cards do alter this
aspect of a bleed), tapping to take the action, etc.

> So, "bleed" is defined
> to be against your prey? In that case, any card which says, "(D)Bleed your

> predator" would be nonsensical. If bleed by definition targets only prey,

> then this whole statement is a contradiction.

Card text can override the definition. [12].

The default bleed is for 1.
The default bleed can be taken by untapped minions only.
The default bleed is directed against the acting minion's prey.
The default bleed doesn't increase your pool.
etc.

Carded bleeds can change these defaults by explicit text.

Computer Hacking changes the first one.
Force of Will changes the first and the second.
Kindred Spirits (inferior) changes the third and fourth.
Kindred Spirits (superior) changes the first, third, and fourth.
Legal Manipulations (inferior) changes the first.
Legal Manipulations (superior) changes the first and fourth.
Night Moves changes the third.

and so on.

Computer Hacking doesn't change the third (or any of the others
except the first).

modifying the rules in a way that makes sense. "(D)Bleed your predator"
takes a statement which you are saying has inherent restrictions "prey" and
adds a new directive which cannot be followed. It doesn't cancel the old
directive or modify it, but simply adds a new one. You are now instructed to
do something to your predator which will cause your prey to lose 1 pool.

block, but your prey loses pool if successful? If not, why not? The actual

sense. If there were a Reaction card that said "This card may not be used
while a minion controlled by another methuselah is acting," we would have a
problem with a contradiction. If card text takes precedence, then this card
could never be played. If "bleed" works like this, then many aspects of the
game simply don't make sense. IMNSHO, "bleed" does not work like this, which
is the only reason that some things that we currently take for granted
actually work (like bleed bounce and a back-bleed Night Moves).

> as per all normal actions. The absence of the (D) in the above
> text indicates that normal rules concerning blocking take effect.

Not so. The (D) identifies actions that are (usually) directed.
It's presence or absence does not affect make the action directed
or undirected.

If the action is directed, it is directed.
If it is not directed, it is undirected.

This hypothetical card's action is directed (since you cannot
enter combat with your own minions). As such, the card should
have the (D) symbol on it as a reminder that it is directed.

Like Sensory Deprivation, inferior Shepherd's Innocence, and
Trick of Danya.
Those actions are always/usually directed, so they should've had
the (D) symbol on them.

But the absence of the (D) symbol doesn't make the actions
undirected. Those actions are directed if they target another
Methuselah (including cards/counters she controls).

> In the case of
>
> (D) Bleed your predator
>
> The first (D) is reminder text, but also present to bring some
> consistency to the card set (since most actions which target
> other methuselahs or their minions have the (D) symbol.)

Right.

> The Bleed text 'activates' the rules set regarding bleeds,
> modifying them in the targetting section - the bleed must be
> targetted to your predator, instead of the prey.

It has inherent *default* restrictions. "prey" is the default target.
Adding "prey or predator" changes the default restriction to the new
(non-default) restriction (effectively easing the restriction).

This is no more of a problem than if your definition of "(D) Bleed" is
used (that is, "(D) bleed" is defined as "bleed any Methusealh").
With that definition, Night Moves suffers the same problem that you
perceive in the official definition.

Defn Card Problem --------------- ----------------
------------------------------------------- Bleed any Meth. Night Moves
Bleed any Methuselah your prey or predator. Bleed Prey. Computer Hacking
Bleed prey prey or predator.

The solution to both of these, of course, is to allow card
text to override the default definition:

Defn Card Solution --------------- ----------------
------------------------------------------- Bleed any Meth. Night Moves
Bleed your prey or predator. Bleed Prey. Computer Hacking Bleed prey or
predator.

Because the card has allowed you to choose to affect your Predator *instead

OK, try this:

Bleed means "remove pool from the target". [1] [3.2.2]

Bleed does not imply prey, but the rules book requires that bleed

> Chris,
> This train of argument seems to stem from what I think is your belief
> that the simple statement "Bleed your Predator" is insufficient

> There is in CCG's a desire for brevity (due to a lack of much space on

> above statement ("Bleed your Predator"), it would need to be worded as
> follows,
>
> "Bleed your Predator. This card allows you to override the
> restriction of bleeding only your prey."
>

Not at all. Those who have responded to my argument have completely missed
the point. It is not a case of the rules saying "You may only declare bleed
actions against your prey." If they said this, there would be no problem. A
card which said "Bleed your predator" would work fine, because it
specifically overrides the restriction.

The point is, the rules *do not* say you may only bleed your prey. Not at all
explicitly, and only barely do they imply this. LSJ's (and others') argument
that ct-bleeds are against the original intent of the game rests on the
statement that the absolute definition of bleed involves prey.

Let's try another example, and see if you can at least understand where I'm
coming from.

"Defeather." I don't know if that's a real word, but it doesn't matter. Let
us define "defeather" to mean "to remove the feathers from a bird." Now, if
I were to instruct you to "Defeather a bird," you would understand. If I
were to tell you "defeather [something]," you would basically understand me
and if you followed my instructions, you would find a bird and defeather it.
However, if I were to instruct you to "defeather a salamander," you would
have a problem. Defeather is defined to only work against birds. A
salamander is not a bird. How can you possibly follow my instruction?

Thus, my argument that "bleed" is not defined to only work against prey. The
bleed that you can declare without a card has the specific restriction that it
only works against prey. The word "bleed" does not have that restriction,
because it is not given that restriction in the rules. A card which gave such
a restriction would only work against your prey. Since the rules nowhere
specify that a bleed may only be declared against prey, we are left with the
idea that a bleed without a restriction may be directed anywhere.

If LSJ's argument were true, all cards that said "(D) Bleed your predator"
(or anything to that extent) would need to read, "(D) Bleed, but your
predator (and only your predator) may block this action. If successful, your
predator loses pool instead of your prey." Or perhaps "Switch places with
your predator's predator. Bleed. Then switch places with your prey's prey."

-Chris

Okay, so where in the rulebook does it say that any carded bleed
action may be directed at any Methuselah? This all comes again from a
rulebook that was designed to teach people a game, rather than being
used as a rules encyclopedia. I think that if some people had their
way, all CCG rulebooks would read like lawbooks. But hey, then only
lawyers would play... That's my take on these arguments, anyway. If
there's any convincing to be done, it'll come from the arguments about
the playablity of c-t bleed, rather than from rulebook interpretation.
That said, there is some text covering bleeds in the rulebook, and
your arguments seem to bypass them by a lack of specific text in the
rules for carded bleed actions.

omnidirectable. Nor does text on directed actions have any provision
for suspending the restriction on bleeds being only towards the prey.
There is, however specific text in the rulebook that covers bleed
actions in general. Since this is the only text we have, its the only
text that we can apply to bleed actions, carded or not. Other
interpretations are mostly based on the standpoint that if it isn't in
the rules, its legal. That's a faulty interpretation to have, and you
won't find a single CCG maker that would support it, except for maybe
Steve Jackson Games ;-)
Considerations for including c-t bleed in the rules are a different
story, I don't personally support them, but I see arguments for their
inclusion as a more sound method of argument than saying "there's
nothing in the rulebook that says I can't..."

> and you gain the Edge."
>

That's section 6.4.

The section you quoted from memory (very well, I might add), actually goes
like this:

A minion controlled by a Methuselah attempts to reduce
the blood pool of another Methuselah. The term "bleed" is
actually a metaphor. It describes meddling in the affairs
of Methuselahs by paying bribes, burning down property,
spreading rumors, and so on. To have one of your minions
commit a bleed action:

1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your
minion is attempting to bleed.
2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful
in their attempts to stop you, your prey burns one pool.
There are also cards that allow your minions to bleed your
prey for more than one pool.

But, either way (your by-memory quote or the actual quote), the section
indicates that the action is directed at your prey by default.

The last sentence I quoted is particularly interesting to this
discussion. It is just a reminder/paraphrase of the Golden Rule
of Cards, but its use of the term "prey" is again indicative of
the way carded bleeds default to regular (cardless) bleeds (barring
further card text, of course).

> Considerations for including c-t bleed in the rules are a different
> story, I don't personally support them, but I see arguments for their
> inclusion as a more sound method of argument than saying "there's
> nothing in the rulebook that says I can't..."
>

I'm not arguing in favour of c-t bleeds. It may be difficult to follow the
purpose through an entire thread, but I mean only to prove that the "original
intent" in the case of (D) bleeds is ambiguous. Any argument which says
"bleeds were *obviously* meant to go against your prey" also, as far as I can
tell, precludes any means ever being used to have anyone bleed someone
besides their prey. The fact that c-t bleeds have been ruled to not be
allowed is enough, as I grudginly have agreed they are bad for the game. But
the argument that the new ruling follows "original intent" is garbge, as I
have tried to prove. Original intent, difficult to prove in any instance, is
especially flimsy in the case of bleeds, as the only "proof" seems to be an
implication introduced in the intstructions for a cardless bleed, which
assumes that all bleeds will affect your prey.

: and you gain the Edge."

: That doesn't say what you are saying. What am I missing?

From the VtES rulebook on the Rulemonger web page, section 6.4, "Bleed":

"Bleed (no card required): Bleeding is one of the most fundamental directed
actions in the game. A minion controlled by a Methuselah attempts to reduce

the blood pool of another Methuselah. The term "bleed" is actually a
metaphor. It describes meddling in the affairs of Methuselahs by paying
bribes, burning down property, spreading rumors, and so on. To have one of
your minions commit a bleed action:

1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your minion is attempting
to bleed.
2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful in their
attempts to stop you, your prey burns one pool. There are also cards that
allow your minions to bleed your prey for more than one pool.

Your predator will attempt to bleed you out of the game. She will try to
send her minions past yours and reduce your blood pool; your minions can
block these actions to defend you. You then have the opportunity to attempt
to send your remaining minions past your prey's minions. If you succeed in
getting through, you can then bleed your prey. You may do damage to your
opponent's minions, but you want to ultimately bleed other Methuselahs out
of the game.

Important rule: Whenever a minion successfully bleeds a Methuselah, the
controller of that minion "gets the Edge"." [end citation]

Note that this tells you how to take a cardless bleed action,
says that it's directed against your prey, and that if you succeed

your prey burns one pool.

In [1.1], under the heading "The Edge Counter", it says "A player who
successfully "bleeds" another Methuselah and reduces his victim's
blood pool gets the Edge." If this isn't the citation LSJ had in
mind for section 1, I'm not sure what it was.

At [3.2.2], he may be thinking of the sentence under the heading
"Action Modifier Cards", which says "For instance, if your minion
is taking a "bleed" action to drain the blood pool of another
Methuselah, you could play an action modifier card designed to
increase the amount of pool you drain."

A citation LSJ didn't give, but which may be useful, is the entry
in the Rules Glossary for "Bleed": "An action that involves one of
your vampires making a direct assault on the pool of another player."

Josh

jyhad one)

But it doesn't say anything to the effect of "Bleeds cause a methuselah pool

I suppose this argument is getting tedious, as most rules arguments that last
more than 2 or 3 posts, but I really don't like the fact that "it's the
original intent" is being used to uphold the new ruling against ct-bleeds,

Well, I guess I will now respond to my own post after seeing everyone
elses. The groups I have played with *have* played with victory points
but really didn't pay much attention to them. The last person around
was generally considered the winner unless it was obvious they didn't
(ie. played a total defensive game and only ousted the last guy). We
all just frown on anyone sitting and only defending - its boring. For a
tournament were it is important to deside *exactly* who the winner is I
would always use VPs - that is the rule after all. We just don't care
all that much. It never does quite feel like a "win" when you were
ousted though, no matter who did it. I think what we "really"
considered a win was both the most VPs *and* being the last at the
table. If you were ousted - that just doen't quite cut it.

losses. (ie. 2 VPs as opposed to 1). I have always considered 2nd place
to be the first loser. (after I get knocked out, I do feel better if I
at least got someone before I went though).

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 27 Aug 1998 ber...@cco.caltech.edu wrote:

> I'm not arguing in favour of c-t bleeds. It may be difficult to follow the
> purpose through an entire thread, but I mean only to prove that the "original
> intent" in the case of (D) bleeds is ambiguous.

I do not believe such a position is defensible. The original state of the
rules is quite clear. If you do not mind, I will present the situation to
you anew. I'm not sure I am saying anything you have not heard already,
but perhaps a coherent chronological account will be more convincing than
alot of snippets.

Let's start with Jyhad.

Section 12.3.1 of the Jyhad rulebook describes bleeding

Bleed (no card required): [...snip metaphorical descriptions of
bleeding...].
You may attempt to bleed the player who is your prey by declaring
a bleed action. If unblocked, this action, this action removes one
blood from the blood pool of the bled player to the blood bank. If
your vampire has a modifier to its bleed, it may remove extra blood
from your prey to the blood bank.

Note that, while it says no card is required, this text does not say it
applies only to cardless bleeds. Obviously, it is intended to apply to
all bleeds, or otherwise there would be no rules to say what carded bleeds
do. Naturally, carded bleeds will change and alter what bleeds normally
do, or otherwise there would be no point to them. Thus, "Computer
Hacking", says "(D) Bleed at +1." which means--follow the rules for
(cardless) bleed actions, except that your target will lose an additional
pool.

It ought to be clear that the rule that bleeds target your prey remains in
effect, unless there is card text to contradict that. The rules say,
quite clearly, that a "bleed" targets your prey. The rules also
state that card text can break the base rules.

There is no card text on "Computer Hacking" which states that this
particular bleed does not have to target prey...that is, unless that
mysterious (D) symbol can be taken as meaning something to this effect. I
move on to that subject.

A listing of "Jyhad Symbols" on the back of the rules booklet clearly
indicates that (D) means "Directed Action".

In Section 13.3.1 (Who May Block Whom) one learns what "directed actions"
are.

Actions that directly affect another Methuselah are called *directed
actions* and can only be blocked by that Methuselah's minions. Other
actions are called *non-directed* and can be blocked by either your
predator's or prey's minions.
Directed actions are noted on action cards with a (D) symbol in
the card text. If the (D) symbol does not appear, it is not a
directed action. The only directed actions that do not require a card
are bleeding and encountering another Methuselah's vampire in torpor.

Thus, it appears that the (D) symbol does not change anything about the
bleed, since even cardless bleeds are directed. It's presence on the card
is redundant. The card could have merely said "Bleed at +1" and had the
same meaning, since the word "bleed" in and of itself is sufficient to
indicate that the action is directed.

The reason why the symbol is there is simple: The game designers are
trying to be consistent in putting the symbol on all Action cards that
describe directed actions, so that one will be able to tell by its absence
that the action in non-directed. That intent is clearly stated in the
above-quoted section.

Thus the (D) symbol says nothing about who the target is. It merely
indicates that the minions of the target Methuselah (whoever he is) can
block, and no one else can.

If this is not clear enough, let us look at the evidence of the cards
themselves. There are two bleed cards in Jyhad that explicitly over-ride
the restriction of bleeding one's prey only: Night Moves and Cat
Burglary.

Night Moves
<Action> <Obfuscate>
(D) Bleed your predator or prey at +3 stealth. If more than one

pool is bled with this action, ignore the excess.

*(D) As above but at +6 stealth.*

In light of later rulings, the "predator or prey" text had been
interpreted as a restriction preventing one from bleeding accross the
table as the (D) symbol was then interpreted as normally allowing. The
text was actually intended to grant a special privilege. The original
interpretation seems more appropriate to the card, as it is hardly
overpowered enough for a cross-table bleed restriction to be justified, or
even meaningful. Those who dread cross-table bleeds are hardly going to
breathe easier knowing that they are safe from Night Moves.

Cat Burglary
<Action> <Celerity>
*+1 stealth*
(D) Bleed, but if more than one pool is bled with this action,
ignore the excess.
*(D) Bleed any Methuselah, but if more than 1 pool is bled with
this action, ignore the excess.*

This card is convincing evidence that carded bleeds were never intended to
normally permit the bleeding of any Methuselah, (D) symbol or no. The
only difference between the inferior and inferior version of this card is
that the Superior explicitly allows the bleeding of "any Methuselah".
The inferior version has no explicit restriction preventing this, but
merely fails to explicitly allow it -- just like Computer Hacking.

If inferior Cat Burglary is interpreted as only allowing bleeding of one's
prey (as it clearly must be--for otherwise the superior and inferior
versions are identical), then to be consistent, Computer Hacking must be
interpreted similarly.

Cat Burglary is rare card. It was intended to do something rather usual
and special (*if* you had Superior Celerity), by overriding the
restrictions on who you could bleed, just as Eagle's Sight, at superior,
was able to over-ride restrictions on what actions one was allowed to
attempt to block.

Another card I might mention is Arson:

Arson
<Action>
*Do not replace until after combat.*
(D) Burn a location. Can be directed at any Methuselah.

Surely, if the (D) symbol meant what is was later claimed to mean, then
this last sentence would have been entirely superfluous. It's kinda
superfluous anyway, but...

--------------------------

Sometime between the release of Jyhad and the release of V:tES, a ruling
was issued on the meaning of the (D) symbol. Actually, it would be more
proper to call the ruling errata, since it clearly altered what the (D)
symbol was originally intended to mean.

The ruling stated that the (D) symbol indicated that an action could be
directed at any target, unless there was explicity card text indicating to
the contrary.

The main effect of this ruling was to allow cross-table bleeds with
bleed-boosting actions. It served no other purpose. All other action
cards that had the (D) symbol were fairly clear in defining who their
target was.

I have no idea why this errata was issued. I can only assume that the
person responsible was used to doing CT bleeds, wanted to continue to do
it this way, and wanted everyone else to do it the same way he did
regardless of what the rulebook said or the game designers intended.

Some other residual effects:

Cat Burglary now required errata, for otherwise the inferior and superior
versions were identical. In September 1994 errata was issued saying that
"The inferior version is directed but not (D)."

This errata must have been confusing for those who took the rulebook at
its word and assumed that "directed" was precisely what the (D) symbol was
supposed to signify. It is annoying also to have a symbol that cannot be
pronounced out loud while still preserving what is now supposed to be its
full meaning. It reminds me of that silly unpronounceable symbol that
the Artist Formerly Known As Prince has taken to insisting is his name. I
can understand TAFKAPs desire to make himself seem mysterious, but I
cannot understand why one would want to do this with the Jyhad rules.

As one can imagine, this ruling made a lot of people want to slap the
rules team silly. Thankfully, it has now been reversed, and the rules
restored to their original state of elegance.

One of the consequences of this ruling was that Cat Burglary became one of
the most despised of all rares, the one most commonly cited as an example
of the fact that rares cards in Jyhad are not necessarily better than
commons. Instead of being an (otherwise underpowered) bleed card that
grants a rare privilege at superior, it became an underpowered bleed card
that has unusual restrictions at inferior.

-----------------------

Finally, I will discuss the release of the V:tES edition of the rules.

V:tES was released long after this strange ruling, and while it was still
in effect. Oddly enough, the new ruling was not incorporated into the
latest addition of the rules, and nothing can be found in the V:tES
rulebook that supports or acknowledges it. I do not know if this was an
oversight, or deliberate behavior on the part of one who did not agree
with the current ruling.

In section 6.3.1, where Directed Actions are defined:

Cards that involve directed actions have a (D) in the card text. The
only directed action in the Basic Game that does not require a card is
bleeding.

And in section 18.1

Directed Actions directly affect another Methuselah or one of his
minions. They may only be blocked by the minions of that Methuselah.
Directed actions are noted on cards with a (D) in the card text.

Again, the purpose of the (D) symbol is to identify a "directed action" so
it can be determined who is allowed to attempt to block. No other purpose
is indicated.

Under 6.4 (Minion Actions):

Bleed (no card required): Bleeding is one of the most fundamental

directed actions in the game. [...snip metaphorical description of
bleeding...]. To have one of your minions commit a bleed action:

1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your minion is
attempting to bleed.
2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful in their

attemps to stop you, your prey burns one pool. There are also cards

that allow your minions to bleed your prey for more than one pool.

Note again that it is not stated that the above applies only to cardless
bleeds. Bleed action cards are handled precisely as above, with the only
difference being that you play the bleed card as the action is announced
(as is done for all carded actions), with card text as always modifying
the base rules.

Note also how the last sentence takes care to indicate that one's prey is
still the target even when cards are involved. The words "your prey" are
not necessary to the sentence, and I cannot help wondering if they were
put in deliberately by a writer that disagreed with the then-current
ruling.

In the V:tES edition, there was only one acknowledgement of the
then-current ruling, and it was not in the rulebook. Rather, Cat Burglary
was corrected, in accordance with then-current errata lists, such that the
(D) symbol at inferior was removed.

Note that, with the (D) gone, this card now violates the promise make in
the rulebook that directed actions will be identified by the (D) symbol.
It should have been revised to say "(D) Bleed your prey..."

Nonetheless, the V:tES text has been cited by persons in this NG as
evidence that the (D) symbol was originally intended to allow for bleeding
any target... thus it's conspicuous absence in the inferior version of Cat
Burglary.

I trust this little history puts the matter in a better perspective.

Lupus Australis

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 27 Aug 1998 ber...@cco.caltech.edu wrote:
> I'm not arguing in favour of c-t bleeds. It may be difficult to follow the
> purpose through an entire thread, but I mean only to prove that the "original
> intent" in the case of (D) bleeds is ambiguous.

In that case, you are clearly wrong. I can understand why some people
would want CT bleeds. Perhaps they, unlike me, are very good at games
like Diplomacy and Risk. Perhaps they, unlike me, find the kingmaker
effect ("may the best man lose") to be amusing. I, however, am an
introvert who has trouble with social strategy. This is a matter of
taste.

However, it is absolutely clear from the Jyhad rulebook, the V:tES
rulebook, and other available evidence that all bleeds were intended to
target one's prey only unless card text explicitly indicated to the
contrary.

> Any argument which says "bleeds were *obviously* meant to go against
> your prey" also, as far as I can tell, precludes any means ever being
> used to have anyone bleed someone besides their prey.

I don't see why. The game designers *obviously* meant for only the
targetted Methuselah to be able to block a directed bleed, since they
wrote a rule explicitly stating this. This however did not stop them from
designing the card "Eagle's Sight" to overcome this restriction.

> The fact that c-t bleeds have been ruled to not be allowed is enough, as
> I grudginly have agreed they are bad for the game. But the argument

> that the new ruling follows "original intent" is garbage, as I have
> tried to prove.

Well, in that case I have just written a long post of "garbage" under the
heading "Original Intent". Please read it and let me know if you are
convinced.

> Original intent, difficult to prove in any instance, is especially
> flimsy in the case of bleeds, as the only "proof" seems to be an
> implication introduced in the intstructions for a cardless bleed, which
> assumes that all bleeds will affect your prey.

There are no instructions for a "cardless bleed". There is an instruction
for bleeds, an basic action that does not require an action card (but
does not preclude one either).

Action cards that instruct you to "Bleed" are handled according to the
same rules. Indeed, there would be no point at all in using the word
"Bleed" in the card text at all if the intent was not to refer you to
these rules. Cart text will tell you how the bleed will be different than
normal. This will change or modify the rules somewhat, of course, but
this is true of any card you play.

If the V:tES bleed rules do not apply to carded bleeds, then I have no way
of knowing what a carded bleed does. Perhaps Computer Hacking removes
blood from a minion rather than from Methuselah's pool? If I am going to
ignore what the rules say a bleed does (on the grounds that they only
apply to "cardless bleeds") then this seems the most reasonable assumption
-- since "bleed" seems to associate better with "blood" than with "pool".



> least be supported beyond a reasonable doubt. My only goal is to show that
> original intent is not obvious.)

Same thing, only clearer. I thought we were discussing the current
rules/rulebook, not the original intent, sorry.

Jyhad rulebook:

12.3.1. Minion Actions

You may attempt to bleed the player who is your prey by declaring

a bleed action. If unblocked, this action removes one blood from

the blood pool of the bled player to the blood bank.

--

And, as an aside, what's the reason for treating "default" as
"default if no card is used"?

"Default" is intended to apply by default. That is, unless
something explicitly changes the default.

If, when I bleed, I can bleed only my prey (by default), then
why is it that, when I have a card that says "bleed" suddenly
I can bleed anyone I choose. What has changed to override the
default?

He was talking about the Jyhad version, not the messed-up V:tES version.

The V:tES version is messed up, because the rulebook (Jyhad and V:tES)
promises that all directed actions are supposed to have this symbol. This
remained in effect despite the (erroneous) ruling that the (D) symbol, by
default, indicates that the bleed can effect anyone. It should have said
"(D) Bleed your prey..." and card text would have been adequate to
over-ride this ruling (as it does in a great many cards), while still
making it clear that this was a directed action.

In the Jyhad version the inferior says "(D) Bleed,...." while the Superior
says "(D) Bleed any Methuselah,...." Otherwise, the superior and inferior
versions are identical.

had a whole bunch of restrictions because Celerity was already a really great

> Bleed (no card required): Bleeding is one of the most fundamental
> directed actions in the game. [...snip metaphorical description of
> bleeding...]. To have one of your minions commit a bleed action:
>
> 1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your minion is
> attempting to bleed.
> 2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful in their
> attemps to stop you, your prey burns one pool. There are also cards

But the card played isn't described above. If you want to read this stuff
literally, then you must read it completely literally. There is no step
above where an action card may be played. You simply tap the minion and
announce you are attempting to bleed.

On the other hand, when declaring an action with a card from hand, you tap
your minion, play the card and follow the instructions on the card. The card
just says bleed, not "bleed your prey." It doesn't say anything about
following the rules for a cardless bleed, it only does that which is
fundamental and inseparable from the word "bleed," i.e. (D) action, remove
pool if successful, gain edge if successful. Since the target is not
inherent in the word "bleed," no target is specified, unlike the cardless
action.

Hehe... "Ned and Jimbo Huntin' Game." I think I'm gonna market that. And

have any rules that describe how to do that. 8)

> I don't see your point here, at all. It is fairly antithetical to the entire

Okay, let's take the analogy a little closer to the source material. What if
there were a card that said, "(D) Enter combat with one of your minions."
Further, let's assume that this is back in the day when (D) actions couldn't
be directed at yourself.

Okay, we *could* interpret this. First off, directing a (D) action against
one of your minions is a problem, but we'll just interpret that to mean that
no one may block the action without Eagle's Sight, etc. This is consistent
with the self-directed Rampage ruling. Next, we must break the rule that
your minions cannot enter combat with each other. Okay, so they do. I'm not
sure how, and I'm not really sure about the mechanics. Can the minion you're
entering combat with play Reaction cards? What about Action Modifiers? I
suppose not, since it's your turn and he's not acting. What if he plays Mask
of 1K Faces on the action? (Okay, that last one isn't fair, because nothing
similar exists in the "bleed your predator" case, but it's fun to think
about...) Now you're in combat. Something in one of the rulings says that
if 2 minions controlled by the same methuselah are in combat together, combat
immediately ends. Does that happen in this case? Because the card is
specifically instigating a combat between two of your minions, is it alright
if we break that rule (note that the card doesn't *say* it is breaking that
rule, so what do we do)? What about playing a card to look at the opposing
methuselah's hand? Do you look at your hand? I guess so. Sure, we can
probably figure out what to do, and even make sense out of the card, but it's
not easy, and someone else might have a different interpretation.

If "prey" is included in "bleed," then I say that a strict adherence to the
rules will lead to similar problems. If bleeds can *ever* be directed at
anyone else, then "(D) Bleed" (with or without the (D) symbol; I don't want
anyone else trying to instruct me that the (D) symbol is just a reminder... I
know it is) would imply an omni-directable bleed. This is easily solved by
ruling that bleeds are directed at prey only by default, but that's *not*
original intent. The original rules do not and cannot restrict where
unrestricted bleeds are directed, and thus original intent cannot be proven
from the rulebook.

That's what my argument is.

lose? If they are attacking you it is to make you lose you most
valuable vampire (most of the time).

> So powerful vote decks dominate, but people don't paly with vote defence
> cards?

No, powerful vote decks do not dominate. Neither do bleed decks, or
rush decks, etc... If they did then maybe enough people would use these
cards to make them usefule.

> > You're right. What I meant to say was that I am usually ready to block
> > a bleed (intending from my pred but could be from anywhere). It's true
>
> Even if they dumped a single stealth card on it? say +2 stealth with LiC?

> stealth is probably the minimum any decent bleed deck would consider.

I'll agree with you here. It is very difficult to stop any focused deck
at its primary ability. Its hard to fight a rush deck, its hard to stop
a vote deck passing a vote (although easier now), and its hard to catch
a steath bleed deck. The later has always, IMO, been a little
unbalanced because it is good at the only thing you *really* need to be
good at but that has little to do with cross table bleeds.

A little aside to the comment I wrote above: if the reason people don't
want ct-bleeds is because it gives one more tool to those stealth bleed
decks then I guess it might be a good idea. I generally don't see that
perspective right away because my group stopped using focused stealth
bleed decks long ago because they are *boring*. Its just not fun to
play one. One will pop up once in a while and not be used again.
Because of this, I am looking at this whole argument a little skewed
(and I admit it). Without the need to limit steath bleed decks, this
just becomes: taking a useful (but not focus, so not to powerful) tool
away from other decks. So please, someone let me know if the crux of
this has to do with limiting stealth bleed decks.

> I don't care whether you are ousted, a single CT bleed can take away resources
> that you should have been able to use to hold off your predator. And I don't
> understand your insistence that non-ousting CTBs are justified.

I'm not saying justified or not, I simply saying that losing a minion is
often just as bad.

> > Again, this is just different from my experience where the reaction vote
> > cards are seldom used.
>
> If they exist, and your group is not using them, this is not an excuse for not
> using them. These cards easily stymie vote decks, and are readily available -
> unlike the bleed defenses, which require disciplines.

They only easily stop vote decks if *many* people use them. I can throw
all the suprise influence I want into my hand but that two votes just
won't help against a good vote deck (although it may help more with no
vote push.) This is obviously a metagame issue because if everyone
played with them then I could see them being useful. That takes up a
lot of card slots when you also have to "hope" that someone else uses
them too.

> Remember that by using any of these bleed cards, you are having an effect
> equal to two or more (many more!) single action bleed.

good point.

> > design your deck to effectivly be able to bleed anywhere and this really
> > doesn't pay off. Therefore c-t bleeds are an occational tool you can
> > use to help your situation (I am disregarding random c-t bleeds which I
> > agree are anoying).
>
> But CTB can be beyond annoying. You and I agree that it has a minimal
> strategic impact for the acting meth (except in certain circumstances, where
> you are taking advantage of something that is not in the original rules, to
> gain a strategic advantage which you should have had to gain through
> competition or diplomacy), and you agree that idiots can abuse it (whether it
> is for spite, out of game reasons, or other irrelevancies), you say that you
> rarely use it, so _why_ should we keep it? Particularly since it was not part
> of the original game, and gives an unfair advantage to a particular deck
> strategy?

You might be right, and I guess I am willing to give it a try to see how
it plays. I have only recently begun to agree that it may have been the
original intent (please don't start that argument again - it is already
discussed to death). I only have one idiot I play with occationally
(and we usually don't let him) so that is not a big deal for me. Is the
deck strategy you refer to a focused stealth bleed? If so I probably
agree, although it has been a long time since I saw one that was any
good - I don't play tourn. and nobody around here likes to play them.
Anyway, like I said, you may be right.

Kevin

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Kevin Kelly (kke...@atlantic.net) wrote:

: I still say that losing a minion *can* be a much bigger detriment than

: losing some blood. This is very situational but I think I can come up
: with at least as many situations where losing a particular minion is
: much more detrimental in the long run than losing some blood.

But 'losing' the minion only applies (I think) when the vampire is
actually burned, since if it's only torporized it can come back
relatively easily. Burning a vamp takes even more 'work' (in terms
of cards used etc.) than sending it to torpor, and as in my previous
comparison of bleeds vs combat, it seems to me that torporizing takes
at least as much 'work' as performing a large bleed.

: Arguable either way. Against a good rush, they will fight someone, the

: most you can hope for is to pick who and hopy you have the defenses.
: Against a big bleed, besides the normal defenses, you can always block
: it and other than bruise and bleed decks if blocked there probably won't
: be a big fight.

Most bleed decks I've seen try to have some method of not being blocked,
except for bruise/bleed decks.

: I'll agree with you here. It is very difficult to stop any focused deck

: at its primary ability. Its hard to fight a rush deck, its hard to stop
: a vote deck passing a vote (although easier now), and its hard to catch
: a steath bleed deck. The later has always, IMO, been a little
: unbalanced because it is good at the only thing you *really* need to be
: good at but that has little to do with cross table bleeds.

: bleed decks long ago because they are *boring*. Its just not fun to

: Because of this, I am looking at this whole argument a little skewed
: (and I admit it). Without the need to limit steath bleed decks, this
: just becomes: taking a useful (but not focus, so not to powerful) tool
: away from other decks. So please, someone let me know if the crux of
: this has to do with limiting stealth bleed decks.

It doesn't for me; I can't speak for anyone else.

Regarding the boringness/effectiveness of focused stealth bleed decks:
This is a classic 'problem' with 4-card-limit games. If you're playing
no limits (I don't know if you are), focused stealth bleed decks are
typically extremely vulnerable to well-constructed combat decks (especially
Immortal Grapple combat decks). If you don't have highly effective
combat decks in your group, that could be what causes stealth bleed
to seem overly effective.

In my experience, focused stealth bleed decks may be boring to play in
that they tend to be pretty predictable, but they aren't boring in
the sense of being too good, so as to make the game no fun.

I do think it's true that bleed decks of any variety have an advantage
in that they directly attack the primary resource of their prey, and
no one else can typically interfere - that is, the task they specialize
in is the one that gets victory points. But for the most part, they
are still balanced with vote and combat decks in a well-evolved
environment.

Josh

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
ber...@cco.caltech.edu wrote:
> > Bleed (no card required):

> > You may attempt to bleed the player who is your prey by declaring
> > a bleed action. If unblocked, this action, this action removes one
> > blood from the blood pool of the bled player to the blood bank. If
> > your vampire has a modifier to its bleed, it may remove extra blood
> > from your prey to the blood bank.
> >
> > Note that, while it says no card is required, this text does not say it
> > applies only to cardless bleeds.
>
> It implies that it only applies to cardless bleeds, because it is included in
> after "Bleed (no card required)."

You're treating "no card required" as "absence of a card required".
It actually means "a card is not required", and does not exclude
the use of a card.

> *This* bleed, which does not require a
> card says explicitly "Bleed your prey." *Other* bleeds only say "Bleed."
> While you might take the implication that this is meant to be your prey, it
> is about as far from "obvious" as is humanly possible.

Kindred Spirits (inferior) says "(D) bleed any methuselah."
But, it doesn't say for how much.

The default (cardless) bleed removes one pool, but that doesn't apply
here, since this is a card.

Therefore, if the presence of a card means that I can pick any target
I want (in the absence of a restriction in card text, as is the case
for Computer Hacking), then the presence of a card likewise means that
I can pick any amount that I want (in the absence of a restriction given
in card text), right?

Of course not. The default attributes of a bleed are the defaults.
They apply unless some other effect changes the default.

The default is: prey is the target.
The default is: one pool.

> The rules say, quite clearly, that the bleed which does not require a card
> may only target your prey.

It says that the bleed action doesn't require a card.
And it says that the bleed action is directed at your prey.

The cardless action can only target the prey, yes (unless card text
says otherwise - Rafaele Giovanni).

The carded bleed is still a bleed action. That same action that didn't
require a card but that can be done with a card. That same action that
is directed at your prey by default. Unless some effect (like card
text) allows you to bleed some other Methuselah, you can only bleed
your prey, as described in the rules.

> No where is there a clear definition of what
> "bleed" means when it is printed on a card. There is no reason to believe
> that the word bleed contains within it any restrictions, and thus may do
> anything that "bleed" allows. Since "bleeds" can possibly be sent to other
> methuselah's, there's no reason to believe that the word "bleed" restricts
> you to a particular methuselah.

"Bleed", when printed on a card, means the same thing as "bleed" when not.
It is a term. The presence of a card doesn't change the term.

There is no reason to believe that any of the default behavior of a
"bleed" is changed by the fact that the word "bleed" appears on a
card. Quite the opposite, in fact. There is every reason to assume that
"bleed" means "bleed" in all the usual (default) ways, except as
exceptions are noted on card text.

"Bleed" restricts you to your prey because of the rules on "bleed".

> > There is no card text on "Computer Hacking" which states that this
> > particular bleed does not have to target prey...that is, unless that
> > mysterious (D) symbol can be taken as meaning something to this effect. I
> > move on to that subject.
>
> Oh no... not the (D) symbol crap. The (D) symbol is simply a reminder that
> the action is directed.

Not to the people that brought you the "Computer Hacking can be used to
bleed any Methuselah." That ruling was justified by their interpretation
of the rules that said "the (D) symbol gives omni-directability."

That rule/errata is the only way thing that could allow Computer Hacking
to be directable at any Methuselah (outside of card-specific errata, of
course). (As explained by Tom, in <3fsrbe$7...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>, January
1995: "The D symbol overrides the normal rules for who you can bleed." -
note the "normal rules for who you can bleed" part. It is not the card,
but the (D) symbol, that used to allow the change in the default bleed.)

With the (D) symbol as only a reminder, which is now is, Computer Hacking
can only target your prey, as indicated in the rules.

> [Cat Burglary]

> Here you go again, trying to convice me that there are no misprints in Jyhad.

> [...] The best explanation I've heard is that during

> playtesting, they were undecided whether or not to allow ct-bleeds, and when
> they decided in favour, they forgot to change the text on Cat Burglary.

And forgot to change the text in the rulebook, apparently, since that
still said that bleeds are directed at one's prey, and fails to say
that playing a card changes that default behavior, even after three
revisions (Printed Jyhad, Corrected Jyhad, VTES, Corrected VTES).

Again, the old ruling was based on the fact that the (D) symbol itself
granted omnidirectability. That is, the (D) symbol was overriding the
rules on who could be the target of a bleed.

> [snip]

> But the card played isn't described above. If you want to read this stuff
> literally, then you must read it completely literally. There is no step
> above where an action card may be played. You simply tap the minion and
> announce you are attempting to bleed.
>
> On the other hand, when declaring an action with a card from hand, you tap
> your minion, play the card and follow the instructions on the card. The card
> just says bleed, not "bleed your prey." It doesn't say anything about
> following the rules for a cardless bleed, it only does that which is
> fundamental and inseparable from the word "bleed," i.e. (D) action, remove
> pool if successful, gain edge if successful. Since the target is not
> inherent in the word "bleed," no target is specified, unlike the cardless
> action.

The amount is also not inherent in the word "bleed". So, by your argument,
it could be for any amount (unless card text specifies an amount).

Fortunately, that's not how it works.
You bleed your prey by default.
You bleed for one by default.
Card text is required to change these defaults.

--

like Elder Kindred Network and Political Backlash can then come into effect.
Admittedly, if only one player uses them, they are weak, but if 2+ players
use them, voting can quickly become dicey, with 2+ pool losses and more. This
is without counting Delaying Tactics.

> original intent (please don't start that argument again - it is already
> discussed to death). I only have one idiot I play with occationally
> (and we usually don't let him) so that is not a big deal for me. Is the
> deck strategy you refer to a focused stealth bleed? If so I probably

Generally just Bleed, but S&B is the worst case scenario.

> agree, although it has been a long time since I saw one that was any
> good - I don't play tourn. and nobody around here likes to play them.
> Anyway, like I said, you may be right.

No, concession on my part. I can see that a (D) bleed against ones predator
is a reasonable tactic - It falls within the pred-prey "Original Intent" as
well. And while the strategic benefit is questionable, I don't think it is
remarkably abusive. But while I wish it were possible to inflict more than 1

minimalist set of rules without the abusive CTB stuff.

Christopher Chew <c...@id4.telecom.fedex.com> wrote:
> > Christopher Chew wrote:

> > > Hence why I typed the following lines: This game no longer "belongs"
> > > to the designers it belongs to the collective Jyhad community. We are its
> > > lifeblood and its interpreters.

[regarding LSJ as official source]

> So what Official, Unofficial he simply gives an opinion which can and should
> be disputed if a substantial part of the gaming community feel "HIS"
> concepts are in error.

And he has demonstrated an extreme receptiveness to debate on issues that make
the game Jyhad a more balanced one. Whether you agree with these ideas or not
is irrelevant: the forum that he drew the current rulings from (here) has
debated these topics for _years_.

If you don't care about topics of play balance, play at home with your
playgroup you way, but don't expect that your way should become a standard.

If you don't like some _particulars_ of the rules, try to argue rationally on
why a particular should be changed. The current No Repeat Action and Vote
Push rules were changes to the rules that were talked about and debated for
some time before being adopted. There _is_ a history that _shows_ that
well-argued ideas get adopted.

> Years ago D&D did not support the natural 20 double damage rule now they do
> because it was widely used by the gaming community. Same concept.

Different concept.

The primary difference here is that D&D isn't primarily a competitive game.
For a competitive game, doing this kind of toadying is not a good thing. To
do so is to change the game for reasons that don't necessarily impact the
game in a good way. To do so allows a bunch of players who perhaps learned
the basic game and thought that Steal Blood should burn a vampire the ability
to make this the case, irregardless of its impact on the quality of the game,
simply because they might be louder or more numerous.

The quality of a game is what keeps its players. What you argue for is not
conducive to keeping a high quality game. Allowing debate and change in
the game based on that _sound_ debate is what keeps a high quality game.

If you disagreed with the discussions at the time, you should have
spoken up when they were being discussed. The arguments for most of the
recent rulings were hashed out a long time ago; a concensus was reached
among the net-people, but the rules team refused to budge. Those of us
who were convinced that the game was better "our way" played with those
rules in our own groups. We did so with the knowledge that if we ever
played in a tournament setting, we would have to conform to the official
rules, even if we didn't agree with them. The problems with the rules
could be exploited, and many people who went to tournaments chose to do
exactly that (note that an abusive RtI deck won at Origins 97). But
since we couldn't convince the rules team that we were right, we had no
other choice.

Does this sound familiar? The only difference is that the current rules
team (LSJ et al.) is more open to input from the community-at-large. He
has said repeatedly that if you can find a problem with the rulings,
some point where the game is still unbalanced under the rules, he will
consider changing them. See also his reply (to you, I believe)

I have been trying to get this point across for months now; here goes
again. What's good for the goose is not necessarily good for the
gander. Just because you would have fun playing the game one way

> Same concept. Jyhad is analagous to a roleplaying game using the strictures of
card
> text.

Actually, he's mainly correct. A closer analogy could be taken from M:T$. A
few years ago, it became the rage (in my area, at least), to play "Super
Games." In these, games, you started with 10 cards in hand, drew 2 cards a
turn, had no hand limit, and could play unlimited land per turn. I could
have argued at the time (if I had cared) that Magic should switch to this
system, because it was what players were playing. That was ridiculous,
however, because a) MOST players were not playing that way, and b) it made
the game worse. The fact is, playing in that way virtually assured a
one-turn kill, as whichever player got a Channel/Fireball on the first turn
would win.

This is an example of rule that had some popularity, but was not adopted by a
game, because it was stupid.

NRA/No vote push are examples of rules that helped the game and were adopted.
These are closer in analogy to your D&D rule.

-Chris
